items.title: Street Fighter Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
There’s an infectious and celebratory energy coursing through Kitao Sakurai’s Street Fighter at every turn… Psycho Power, you could say. And “Psycho Power” is an apt metaphysical concept to have so front-and-center of the movie’s plot, because as Capcom’s roster of colorful and strange lowercase “c” combatants strut their stuff and pull off their special moves in hyperkinetic fashion, the movie increasingly feels disconnected from any sense of reality, even its own. Is that really a problem when you’ve got martial arts warriors and demons throwing fireballs, green monsters with Jason Momoa’s face rolling around, or Eric Andre screaming through a bullhorn at the top of his lungs? As it turns out, yes. But, as you quickly learn while watching it, Street Fighter never lets good sense get in the way of a good time.

Street Fighter gets off to a stylish start with a wonderfully executed anime prologue that sets up the divide between protagonists Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken (Noah Centineo), martial artists who’d grown to be best friends while training under their master Gouken (Don Lee). As Ryu fades into obscurity, Ken becomes a pop culture mainstay who can never quite shake the idea that his former friend was the better fighter after Ryu demonstrates an ability to harness “Hado power.” That mystical energy from the spirit realm is only able to be channeled by the greatest warriors, and Sakurai and co-writer T.J. Fixman devote about as many words in their script to explaining it as are included in this very sentence.

More necessary to the plot is how important this ability is to M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), the sadistic leader of the Shadaloo crime organization who stages a tournament of the world’s greatest fighters in hopes of sapping enough Hado power (or Psycho Power, as it’s called around Bison’s office) for him to unlock special moves of his very own. Street Fighter makes a bet that scant few in its audience are going to give two rips about how well-justified its melting pot of characters, magic abilities, and cultural influences winds up, with Sakurai seeming far more intent on representing the franchise as broadly as possible at the cost of telling a deeper story.

The fast and loose nature of the adaptation’s storytelling relies heavily on expected genre tropes for both Ryu and Ken, and that effort falls frustratingly short of how good both Andrew Koji and Noah Centineo are in their respective roles. Between the two, Centineo’s Ken gets more latitude to demonstrate how his attention-starved tenure in Ryu’s shadow has affected him, and Centineo’s restlessness gives Ken a fun “little brother” energy that feels like it goes a lot further to propping up his underdog status within the story than the actual writing of the character does. Ken’s reasons for staying locked into the tournament are never quite clear: Is he here to prove himself against Ryu? To honor his master? To save himself from more MTV Spring Break appearances? To save? Maybe for supporting characters, those reasons are less important. But as one of the two leads and certainly the one with more time in the spotlight, Ken’s motivation could have used a lot more focus, which would’ve allowed for his struggles later in the movie to hit home with the emotional weight the finale seems to be making space for.

Each performer brings inherent strengths to the roles which make up a lot of ground for how underwritten many of them are.

Ryu’s arc has the inverse problem, with a poorly maintained throughline about his struggle with a dark power hiding just under the surface of his otherwise peaceful demeanor. He’s reluctant to engage with the tournament as a result, with that struggle embodied by Roman Reigns’ demonic Akuma, the games character which Street Fighter goes furthest out of its way to justify bringing into the fold here. As great as the Ryu/Ken anime scenes look, Sakurai flashes back to them more and more, which becomes a distracting crutch the movie uses to double back on itself and explain Akuma’s significance to Ryu and Ken’s early days.

It’s a shame, as Andrew Koji is quite compelling as Ryu and does great work keeping the character’s stoicism from drifting into feeling wooden, as often happens with action leads. With how cartoonishly emotive the other characters are, Ryu’s calm is a welcome contrast to whatever weirdo he’s paired up with in any given scene. Perhaps unsurprisingly, Ryu’s intense focus is best juxtaposed against Ken’s manic enthusiasm, and Koji and Centineo are each at their best when bickering with each other. An early fight between the two in a hotel room synthesizes that dynamic best in both performance and action, as Ryu’s one-upsmanship in the duel drives Ken increasingly up a wall. That relatively straightforward fight, and the precise nature of how the camera chases the choreography to accentuate comedic beats, is a bit of an outlier for Street Fighter because the rest of the fights are textbook examples of unchecked maximalism.

Street Fighter never lets too long go by without a brawl breaking out. Whether or not those brawls have any good reason to be happening, the movie certainly kicks into a higher gear when fists are flying, even if the tournament that acts as the backbone of the movie’s second half is pretty much an afterthought. The action blends Hong Kong, anime, and ’80s/’90s movie influences that alternatingly emphasize tight fight choreography and epic hero moments. In that way, ironically, that leaves Scott Pilgrim vs. The World’s video game-inspired action as the closest cinematic relative to Street Fighter’s, a similarity that also makes its way into how the movie’s comedic bent leaves that action needing to function as an engine for both adrenaline and laughs. Sakurai opts for a scattershot approach here, with a tendency to pack action scenes so full with individual gags that often there’s not enough time to fully appreciate them before he’s moving on to the next one. The action is very well-performed by the stunt team and those in the cast like Andrew Koji who are capable of handling the more complicated sequences themselves, but the plot does leave Street Fighter relying more on VFX embellishments to that action as it goes, which add very little to how viscerally it all lands.

The movie’s wide scope does lead to a pretty strong showing from the games’ deep bench of fighters, and the flavor each of their personalities bring to this whacked-out stew are the undeniable highlight of the movie. Through its first half, Street Fighter bends over backwards to introduce game characters like Chun-Li (Callina Liang), Guile (Cody Rhodes), Vega (Orville Peck), Dhalsim (Vidyut Jammwal), and Cammy (Mel Jarnson) and to keep them in the mix as the tournament begins in MetroLao City. These characters’ personal reasons for accepting their invitations become wholly irrelevant after they’re in the door, but Street Fighter is no weaker for that. With no responsibilities to the plot, these fighters are given license to be as bizarre and funny as their individual performers can sustain, and the characters that leave a mark really leave a mark.

Andrew Schulz’s Dan Hibiki, Ken’s replacement best friend after Ryu disappears, is the big surprise on that front. As Ken’s agent, Dan begins the story looking like a money-hungry leech, but his genuine care for his buddy actually becomes one of the few emotional hooks that the movie’s got by the end, and Schulz plays being out of his depth around people who could rock his shit to frequently funny effect. Another comedian who sees big success throughout Street Fighter is Eric Andre, whose emcee Don Sauvage is essentially just a thinly veiled spin on his own signature chaos energy.

From the moment Cody Rhodes’ Guile enters (hair first, of course) to the tune of his absolutely rocking theme song, the strength of his all-American charisma and consistent ability to nail punchlines are let down only by the relatively brief amount of screentime he gets. Others — like Balrog or Zangief — are glorified cameos that at least each add a unique energy to their scenes. Jason Momoa’s Blanka certainly falls into this camp: He’s barely involved, but dang it if the freakish CGI and “Hulked on Phonics” speech pattern that define him don’t leave you leaning in with amused bewilderment by the time he rolls out of the movie. David Dastmalchian’s M. Bison is another reliable source of amusing bewilderment that Street Fighter draws on to great effect: Bison’s relationship to power and just how… gratified he becomes as he creeps closer and closer to attaining it is a surprisingly off-kilter approach to the imposing dictator, and one that Dastmalchian never blinks in the face of.

These characters really exemplify the importance of good casting, as each performer brings inherent strengths to the roles which make up a lot of ground for how underwritten many of them are. That lack of definition does backfire with the most prominent female characters: Callina Liang’s Chun-Li and Mel Jarnson’s Cammy are certainly pretty high up on the list of historically overly sexualized video game characters, a fact Street Fighter doesn’t have an intelligent enough take on to poke fun at without just perpetuating it further. But whether it’s a character rooted in strong cinematic archetypes like Guile or unfortunate ones like Chun-Li, all of the performers wholeheartedly embrace the movie’s ridiculous tone and keep it afloat when the writing lets them down. Street Fighter’s 1990s setting is supposed to be another source of campy energy for the movie, but Sakurai never quite figures out how to effectively channel that nostalgia — little of the production design feels that demonstrative of the period, leaving the way-too-frequent needle drops (including one that released on the whole other end of the decade in which the movie’s set) doing all the heavy lifting on that score.

items.title: SanDisk MicroSD Express Review: Super-Fast Storage for Your Switch 2
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
If you care about raw throughput when picking a microSD Express card, SanDisk’s officially-licensed microSD Express Card for Nintendo Switch 2 may be the one to beat. I’ve been testing one for the last week, and in almost every test I threw at it, it outdid IGN’s current budget pick for the best Nintendo Switch 2 microSD Express card, the Samsung P9 Express.

The real question is whether that’s even worth paying for. MicroSD Express cards are already very fast compared to the older microSD ones still used on every gaming handheld that’s not the Switch 2, and it’s not even close. SanDisk’s card is demonstrably faster in many ways than competing options from PNY and Samsung, but unless you’re transferring game files back and forth between it and your Switch 2, you’re really not going to notice. Faster better, but there are other things to consider, including price.

SanDisk offers its card in 256GB, 512GB, and 1TB capacities. I’ve found 512GB to be the sweet spot, giving you three quarters of a terabyte overall when you factor in the console’s internal 256GB storage. But SanDisk’s cards cost more than similar options from PNY or Walmart’s Onn brand.

When you’re looking at the specs for a microSD Express card for Switch 2, you can safely ignore the main throughput numbers that most manufacturers like to promote. In the case of SanDisk’s card, that’s 880 MB/s reads and 650MB/s writes, which is faster than almost all the other cards I’ve tested! (The only one rated higher is the PNY one, at 890MB/s and 750MB/s, respectively.) But that number refers to the read figure, and as my testing showed, is a poor reflection of actual performance during the reads and writes.

See, video games aren’t monolithic files; they’re packages containing countless smaller files so the process of transferring them is constantly starting and stopping, slowing things significantly. How well a card performs there depends on how it handles these herky-jerky transfers.

Getting a handle on a microSD Express card’s Switch 2 throughput means timing file transfers between it and my console in docked mode. And in that, SanDisk’s card proved super capable. For instance, it reached 94 MB/s when writing Mario Kart World, currently a 22GB game (versus 21.9GB when I tested for the Samsung P9 Express before) to the card. It was actually slightly when it came to moving games back to the Switch 2’s internal storage, only mustering 91MB/s.

That played out the same way for every game I tested. It averaged 105MB/s when I transferred Resident Evil 4 to the card and just 80MB/s on the way back to the console, and I measured 95MB/s to the card and 85MB/s from it when moving Super Smash Bros. back and forth. The 8.9GB Donkey Kong Bananza was the fastest one; it took just over a minute to write the 8.9GB game to the card, making its throughput 122MB/s. (It averaged 88MB/s when I sent it back to internal storage.)

Despite yielding slower reads than writes, SanDisk’s card still outperformed most other cards I’ve tested in most cases. Samsung’s card put up a higher 96MB/s when I transferred Resident Evil 4 from it to my Switch 2 but otherwise ranged between about 1MB/s to 12MB/s slower on other games. The PNY card put up mostly similar read speeds, but managed closer to half the writes of the SanDisk option when it came to write speeds. That could be a difference of minutes on larger files — Mario Kart World took over seven minutes to write to PNY’s card, something that only took about four minutes with SanDisk’s. Basically, if you find yourself shuffling games on and off your Switch 2, the SanDisk microSD Express card could save you real time.

Things equalize where it’s most important: actual loading times for games. Measuring these, I found that the SanDisk card looked almost exactly the same as both the PNY and Samsung cards I tested before. Donkey Kong Bananza took 21 seconds to go from choosing it on the Switch 2’s home screen to its title screen, just like those cards. Mario Kart World averaged 19.4 seconds, or a tenth of a second behind the PNY card and about two seconds faster than the Samsung P9. It got me into The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom nearly a full second faster, at 8.5 seconds, than either of those cards, though.

It’s clear that SanDisk’s officially-licensed Switch 2 card is at least as good as the other high-performing cards on the market, so you won’t be disappointed. It’s still slower than loading games from the Switch 2’s internal storage for the most part, but the difference is negligible – most games only load a fraction of a second faster from the Switch 2 itself than from microSD Express.

items.title: South Park Season 29, Episode 3 Review & Recap: 'You Like That on Your Face'
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for South Park Season 29, Episode 3!

Yeesh, that was probably the weakest new episode of South Park in several years. As is often the case in the show's lesser moments, "You Like That on Your Face" has a few amusing gags and ideas, but none of it comes together as a cohesive whole. Talk about cringe...

This week, the series opts to turn its attention to Gen Z/Gen Alpha culture and hot-button issues like looksmaxxing and aura farming. Honestly, I was really hoping the opening scenes were meant to be a springboard to something else. Yes, aura farming is really stupid and laughable, but did we need an entire episode devoted to the practice?

In execution, "You Like That on Your Face" plays like a spiritual sequel to Season 8's "You Got F'd in the A," only with aura battles replacing the dance-offs of yore. Sadly, this episode compares very unfavorably to its predecessor. It hits too many of the same beats and doesn't really build on its ideas in a satisfying way. I don't know that "Hey, look how stupid and self-absorbed today's kids are" really makes for the greatest material.

This episode also leans way too heavily on the recurring gag of Sephora clerks squirting cream on children's faces and asking, "You like that on your face?" We get it. It's like porn, but with children. It's not particularly funny the first several times, and certainly not by the end when the twisted Sephora manager comes lumbering out of the darkness.

Again, there are some funny bits to be found in Episode 3. The initial reveal of the Sephora Backrooms is pretty funny (though this is another element that doesn't ultimately lead anywhere). The return of the Pet Semetary-spoofing Farmer Ted is also a welcome treat. And Randy himself getting into looksmaxxing and transforming himself into a 4th grader is probably the highlight of the episode. If anything, the South Park team really should have leaned more on that subplot. Randy can usually be counted upon to carry the series, at least when he's not hawking his Tegridy Farms wares. But I suppose we'll see if this particular development carries over into future episodes.

Clearly, despite the series' satirical title change, the intent with Season 29 is to pivot away from the politically focused Season 27/28 approach and return to a more classical brand of South Park that emphasizes the younger characters. That approach worked well enough in the first two episodes, but it falls pretty flat here. I don't know if South America strictly needs to go back to lampooning the Trump administration at every turn, but it does need to develop a more coherent overall storyline for the season and do a better job of tackling the more urgent topics of the day. This isn't it.

items.title: You Can See Everything Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
At nearly three hours in length, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything is a staggering, unnerving documentary about Silicon Valley and whether you can truly know someone. Its focus is Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, who granted the filmmakers unprecedented access for about a month before her prison stint began in 2023. However, the movie is as much about the question of Holmes’ culpability as it is about cults of personality and cultural mythologies at large — not to mention Fielder’s own oeuvre and TV persona as the creator of shows like The Rehearsal, a prankish work of obsession laced with hidden sincerity.

The total here feels greater than the sum of its parts, owing to the allure of its eerie filmmaking and the sheer brain-breaking scope of its ambition as a work of haunting, self-reflexive cinema. Filled with suffocating 4:3 close-ups shot with long lenses, and awash in shadow to disguise motive, the movie’s rapturous form feels like the product of invasive surveillance amidst a mile-a-minute chase. This is despite the fact that most of it is composed of simple, static conversations — a magnificent sleight of hand.

It initially unfolds at a beachside home in San Diego rented by Holmes and her husband, the wild-eyed hotel heir Billy Evans, a man seen voraciously absorbing audio material at double speed. We’re reintroduced to Holmes’ story by way of news clips scoring footage of her daily life, a sort of “previously on” segment detailing her conviction for fraud. However, as an anchor utters the phrase “pathological liar,” the camera falls on Fielder for the first time as he appears like a poltergeist in the corner.

The hilarity of Fielder’s awkward, lumbering presence in this domestic setting — headphones at the ready around his neck like he’s playing the role of “a director” — clashes wildly with unsettling zooms into empty spaces and people’s expressions. As Holmes and Evans raise their two young children, Fielder probes the couple through intimate sit-downs on their couch, and conversations in passing wherever he can steal them.

With the saturation turned up to the edge of uncanniness — in concert with Oppenheim’s Chris Hansen drama from this year, — Holmes’ deep blue eyes become Fielder’s greatest challenge yet, as a man seemingly taken by her charm while also thoroughly unconvinced of her claims that she did nothing wrong. And yet, when it comes to her seemingly magical, test-for-any-disease device, he extends her an enormous benefit of doubt, if only to keep unspooling a tightly-wound thread, thus allowing Holmes and Evans to hoist themselves with their own petards.

As Fielder grows more entwined with the couple, it’s hard not to see the Nathan For You host as if he’s peering into a mirror of sorts. Holmes is a fellow manipulator, though perhaps she’s more adept at it than Fielder is. Fielder’s TV character is that of a slightly naïve and self-effacing man who secretly nudges his subjects in a particular direction through suggestion. But while his goal is entertainment, Holmes’ is securing financial investment, something she continues to work on even as her prison sentence looms.

The visual framing creates a proximity and palpable tension between Fielder and Holmes, but it crafts an equally compelling portrait of Evans as a man potentially pulling the strings. However, the question of whether Holmes is letting him do this or if she’s even aware of what he’s up to remains a central point of inquiry. It’s rare to watch a documentary that gradually becomes about its own making and finances, but these are among its most exhilarating developments; You Can See Everything really does want you to witness its every dimension.

You might find yourself asking why the film occupies such an enormous runtime, but the answer becomes self-evident once it moves into its second half. The question of who Holmes truly is — A deceiver in denial? Someone in the throes of delusion? — remains hauntingly open-ended. This not only imbues the film with a debilitating uncertainty about the kinds of tech moguls running our lives, but it also forces Fielder to turn to a very surprising ally for an alternative peek into Holmes’ mind.

Then again, perhaps this person’s identity is not so surprising if you’re familiar with cultural depictions of Holmes and Fielder’s usual M.O. But the film remains remarkably unpredictable by creating circumstances where people are forced to watch and reflect rather uncomfortably on transcripts and existing footage. Bit by bit, this aforementioned celebrity becomes a kind of co-conspirator in Fielder’s audit of the truth through inviting fireside chats that reveal the gradual frustrations of this particular journey.

As the questions about Holmes and Evans grow more labyrinthine, the movie becomes an astonishing mise en abyme (story within a story) by way of Rehearsal-like re-enactments. These are aimed not only at filling in the gaps caused by Holmes’ incarceration but at using cinematic tools to mine for all possible truths at once to see which one fits… if any at all. It’s exactly the kind of thing you’d expect from Fielder’s experiments, and yet it remains shocking at every turn. At some points, it becomes hard to believe the things you’re seeing and hearing were captured in the first place.

It’s a sympathetic look at a person who, despite the harm she’s caused, seems hell-bent on staying the course and re-enacting the past… not unlike Fielder himself. 

The possibility of the production itself falling apart through the sudden revocation of access always looms, and it certainly isn’t helped by the fact that Fielder is at his most confrontational as an on-screen personality. His provocations are in service of a deeply human search for not only who Holmes is but she is — a mystery that only grows more confounding the more we learn about her, and the closer Fielder gets to her. It’s a sympathetic look at a person who, despite the harm she’s caused, seems hell-bent on staying the course and re-enacting the past… not unlike Fielder himself.

The result is wildly captivating, woven from creeping close-ups and stealthy investigations into the kind of minds making modern tech industries tick. It’s one of the most electric and enrapturing films you’re likely to see this year, and by the time it concludes, its gargantuan 174 minutes may not feel like enough.

items.title: Netflix’s The Diplomat: Season 4 Review
items.author: Michael Peyton
items.content:
Spoilers below for Season 4 of Netflix’s . All episodes are streaming now.

At its core, Season 4 of The Diplomat is a series of one-on-one conversations in which the fate of the world hangs in the balance. The president and vice president, first gentleman and chief of staff, prime ministers, ambassadors, and domestic workers all engage in rich, dramatic dialogue that immediately sucks you in and doesn’t loosen its grip until the season cuts to black. Tight closeups, thick tension, and carefully constructed language imbued with double, triple, and sometimes quadruple meanings unfurl in scene after scene, creating a tapestry of geopolitical and domestic conflict that’s hard to turn away from.

The Netflix series follows American Ambassador to the United Kingdom Kate Wyler (Keri Russell) as she walks the tightrope of managing a simmering international conflict while attempting to save her marriage to her husband, Hal (Rufus Sewell). In Season 4, The Diplomat continues to be a crackling, pulpy thriller with superb writing, gorgeous cinematography, and top-tier performances.

With a new batch of episodes, the show brings what was an already fraught series of storylines to a furious boil. In the aftermath of discovering that President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) colluded with Hal (promoted to vice president in ) to steal an “apocalypse weapon” from a Russian submarine, Kate launches into a campaign of dealmaking and double-crossing to try to get the situation under control. As the season begins, we’re led to believe that the conspiracy will be the central conflict for the foreseeable future. But all of that is quickly scuttled by a harrowing assasination attempt on the president.

The scene, which closes out the premiere episode, is one of the most realistic acts of fictional political violence ever filmed. There’s no music, no building tension; just two quick pops and a shirt suddenly soaked with blood. It's indicative of what The Diplomat does best: presenting the extraordinary as subtle and restrained while still underscoring the global stakes.

This ethos is especially apparent in the still beautifully dysfunctional relationship between Kate and Hal. As the world burns and nuclear conflict is only an itchy trigger finger away, Kate and Hal’s marriage is the spine on which everything else in The Diplomat rests. They’re at once warm with each other yet blisteringly cold, trusting and incredibly suspicious, totally in love but always on the verge of mutually assured destruction. Sewell and Russell continue to be dynamite, layering their scenes together with half-truths, knowing glances, and winking humor. Their on-screen chemistry bursting with intelligence and desire, Hal and Kate often can’t stand each other but would wither away without the other’s counsel.

While Seasons 1-3 of The Diplomat focused mostly on Kate and Hal’s relationship, Season 4 ups Janney’s President Grace Penn and Bradley Whitford’s hilarious but secretly ruthless first gentleman Todd to near co-lead status. Their relationship seethes with a familiarity colored by a brutal imbalance of power. Whitford, in particular, takes full advantage of the show’s darkly comedic writing, imbuing his character with an “aw shucks” brand of humor that belies a knack for cunningly eviscerating anyone who stands between him and his wife. A post-assassination attempt conversation early in the season in which Todd dresses down White House Chief of Staff Billie Appiah (Nana Mensah) is one of those two-handers that highlights the show’s tour de force storytelling and brilliant acting.

As the president, Janney has never been better. Intricately drawn and perfectly performed, Grace Penn is a revelation of a character. Her steeliness and win-at-all-costs attitude of Seasons 2–3 is still intact, but these traits are now forged with a twinge of uncertainty and a whole lot of post-shooting PTSD. As Penn, Janney is at once flighty and megalomaniacal, grounded and borderline mad, caring and absolutely unforgiving. The character knows the consequences of her actions, yet still hasn’t found a line she will not cross. Grace Penn is the most complex, well-drawn president ever put on screen and Janney hits a grand slam in every scene she’s in.

While the four core characters drive much of the show’s drama, The Diplomat features a stacked cast of supporting players who fill out the show’s beautifully crafted world. Ali Ahn and Ato Essandoh shine as Kate’s embassy colleagues Eidra and Stuart. Their budding romance is a twisted mirror of the show’s two other central couples, showing what happens when a relationship heats up after you’re already colleagues instead of vice versa. Rory Kinnear once again chews the scenery to bits as Prime Minister Nicol Trowbridge, especially in a mid-season episode where he’s given a series of fantasy sequences leading up to his blackmail-induced resignation. Doctor Who’s Jodie Whittaker appears late in the season as the new PM, calmly igniting a whole new set of problems for the U.S. government.

Four seasons into The Diplomat, the show’s writing is still obscenely good. Showrunner Debora Cahn and her team of writers synthesize conflicts both personal and global, sprinkle them with a bit of realistic humor, and continually paint the mythological figures at the center of the show as real people.

A scene in the premiere episode shows Kate following the president of the United States into a ladies’ room to press her on an important issue. A storyline, in which Todd (who finagles his way into a London-based job) suspects Kate of being pregnant, unfolds in a way unique to virtually any fictional half-baked pregnancy scenario you can imagine. An international cover-up hinges on whether a team of bureaucrats can convince another team of bureaucrats that they are bad at math. A climactic scene between Grace, Todd, Kate, and Hal that's straight out of Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? is interrupted by an overeager chef. Cahn’s roots in are on full display here. But whereas that show hinged on optimism, The Diplomat subverts that feel-good mentality for realism that’s far more brutal but no less entertaining.

The rest of The Diplomat fires on all cylinders throughout Season 4. Characters walk-and-talk through castle after gorgeous castle. The scenery and cinematography are moody and rich. A late season sojourn to Italy for the G7 summit allows the crew to pull off a series of unbroken long takes that would make David Fincher proud. All of this blends into a spellbinding series of episodes that are pulpy, hilarious, heartbreaking, and downright shocking.

Some of the plot machinations in The Diplomat still can be a bit far-fetched; the show still strains to invent reasons why American government officials need to constantly travel to the UK and some realism is forsaken for the sake of jaw-dropping drama. A few plotlines are even ripped right from the lesser seasons of House of Cards. And yet, it’s still a whip-smart commentary on international politics as they are now. The show forces its audience to reckon with the undeniable truth that the people who run the world are human beings prone to pettiness, stubbornness, and loneliness, and that those qualities often spill over into life-altering decisions for everyone else.

The Diplomat is truly a show for our times, showing how intense, messy relationships — often no more profound than two people talking in a room — can upend lives, transform the mundane into the extraordinary, and have serious consequences for the world at large.

items.title: Slow Horses Season 6, Episode 5 Review — 'Sayonara'
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
This review contains full spoilers for Season 6, Episode 5, which is streaming on Apple TV now.

“Sayonara,” the penultimate episode of Slow Horses Season 6, is just about as close to cinema as a single episode of TV can get… for better and worse. Set largely in foggy countrysides, the wide shots are hauntingly beautiful. It’s got big deaths (bye Jim, drowned in a lake) and twists (Jane survives the car crash!), high-stakes political drama (Diana Taverner’s heated committee hearing), classic spycraft (Jackson Lamb vs. Damien Cantor’s Russian contact), and tender moments between its characters (Sid Baker and River Cartwright, Catherine Standish and Reece Nesmith). Heck, it even ends with a grand gesture and huge car explosion. Slow Horses finally gets its Bond moment.

Oddly, it’s also sort of the antithesis to the series itself; since when do the Slow Horses get to have nice things? River (Jack Lowden) makes awful, nonsensical, emotionally driven decisions that seem to pan out mostly fine. The Horses posted up in Taverner’s country home are gorging on cookies and wine. River and Sid get to kiss, for chrissake! Those fleeting moments, however, are actually a bitter reminder that, no, it usually doesn’t turn out so well for the Slow Horses, as the season sprints to its finale that will, as Frank Harkness and his two minions promise, probably literally burn the house down. Diana Taverner’s holiday home, specifically.

Things pick up seconds after the last episode, where Sid Baker (Olivia Cooke) was kidnapped at gunpoint by confirmed GRU agents Jim (Kyle Soller) and Jane (MyAnna Buring), only now we’re seeing things from River’s perspective as he runs after their car. This really is Sid and River’s Big Episode; Sid uses the “River” novelty plate she bought last episode to slash Jane while driving to save herself from getting killed, even if it did put them all in serious danger when the car does a few barrel rolls and settles upside down. River swoops in to save Sid from being drowned and together they kill Jim.

The pair have a few sweet moments together amid the chaos. River finally tells her about his grandpa’s death. They banter about the most romantic ways to die in a black site hangar. They hornily flirt with each other right before Sid is meant to take off on a Russian plane to Bulgaria — a neutral, untracked place where she’d definitely be killed. And there’s River’s big moment, spurred by the power of a woman being into him: He punches out a few Dogs, steals an airfield maintenance truck, and hands himself over to the cavalcade of black cars to keep Sid from getting caught and sacrificed as retribution for Taverner’s off-book hit in Kazan. Maybe in a different life they could have been together, but it almost definitely won’t be this one.

Speaking of Diana Taverner (Kristin Scott Thomas), the First Desk is imperiously unwavering under scrutiny. There’s Lamb’s (Gary Oldman) reproach, as he’s pieced together that Diana scrubbed the Slough House records because she use the identity of Sid, dead on paper and expendable, to cover up the Kazan assassination. Next is MI5’s all-male oversight committee as she’s questioned about the details of the same hit. In fact, she uses each as opportunities to pontificate about how she has the situation under control and how slow-moving and underfunded the service is. She hasn’t cracked just yet — buttressed by arrogance or necessity, I wonder? — and I’ll be curious to see if she makes it out unscathed or goes the way of all her other predecessors in the finale.

At her holiday home, the merry band of Slow Horses is having a grand old time watching TV, drinking, and prepping Molotov cocktails. Lamb has Roddy Ho (Christopher Chung) digging up dirt on Damien Cantor (Harry Lloyd), but it’s Standish (Saskia Reeves) who finally gets something to do that isn’t staring at wine bottles or being mommy to a gaggle of whiners. Funny enough, it comes at a dinner table moment with Reece (Lenny Rush). Both have been grieving the deaths of not-so-great men they nevertheless had complicated relationships with — Standish, her old boss Charles Partner, and Reece, his dad — and neither would like to talk about it. Yet both play their conversation in a way that feels like they’re getting even just a little solace in finding a tiny amount of common ground.

The biggest curtain pull of the episode is one that we’ve been waiting for an explanation on all season (besides “why erase the Slough House records?”): What the hell is Cantor up to? Though it’s still not 100% clear, we know that he’s been courting mysterious Russian contacts for a media distribution deal, allegedly the biggest in Russian history. (Would he be airing Russian propaganda on his network or making the propaganda for the Russian state-run TV? Maybe both?) But Lamb isn’t far behind. He knows Cantor hired Harkness (Hugo Weaving) to take out Andy Nesmith, Cantor has a strange, regularly scheduled meeting at a children's ballet rehearsal (based on the info gleaned from Ho’s detective work). He tails Cantor’s contact at the theater and then a bookstore, but she loses Lamb — not something a normie could pull off. Now all that remains are the last few pieces of the puzzle left to place.

items.title: Whalefall Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
The new survival thriller Whalefall checked a number of my phobia boxes going into it, so my critical response to the film was always going to be measured by how much it triggered these primal fears of mine. And (I guess?) I’m happy to report the film did that too damn well at times.

Assuredly directed by Brian Duffield and based on Daniel Kraus’ bestselling book of the same name , Whalefall has a simple yet incredibly compelling premise: Young scuba diver Jay Gardiner (Resident Evil’s Austin Abrams) is swallowed by a massive sperm whale and must figure out how to escape from the belly of the beast while his oxygen supply lasts. He has an hour of air left so his struggle basically plays out in real time on screen.

What happens inside the whale’s belly is brought to life with gruesome, excruciating and claustrophobic intensity by Duffield and his team of artists. (They built a whale’s belly, for Jonah’s sake!) There are so many awful ways for Jay to die in there before his oxygen runs out, whether it’s being crushed by the whale’s innards, or succumbing to all the gnarly injuries he sustains from the toxic environment or the other sea creatures the whale has swallowed that are also still alive.

Deeper emotional layers are added to the story by revealing why Jay was diving that day to begin with: He was searching for the remains of his dad, Mitt (Josh Brolin), a well-liked diver and whale-watching boat skipper in their Central California community. Suffering from mesothelioma, which robbed him of being able to dive and connect with nature, Mitt drowned himself in the opening scene rather than continue suffering.

Jay refused to see his father in his final days after a volatile falling out. Jay’s grief and guilt over his strained relationship with his gruff, tough love dad has consumed him and, as he desperately tries to find a way to escape the whale, flashbacks to the lessons Mitt drilled into him about diving and nature prove vital to his slim chances of trying to MacGyver his way out of this ordeal.

Whalefall is a visceral, grueling survival tale, but what distinguishes it in the man vs. nature/beast genre is that it’s really about a father and son who don’t know how to communicate with each other. It’s not until he’s near death himself that Jay starts to truly understand his father and find peace. This makes the third act pretty trippy as the symbolism of the whale and its role in nature is intertwined with Jay’s oxygen-deprived thoughts about Mitt. This device inches right up to the edge of absurdity but thankfully never plummets into it. It’s weird but sincere and moving enough to work.

As Mitt, Brolin is basically Robert Duvall in The Great Santini crossed with Quint from Jaws. He looks like a Hell’s Angel, talks like a New Age hippie, and is basically able to get along with everyone but his son. In the hands of a less skilled actor, the character could have been unbearable but Brolin makes him flesh and blood and, ultimately, vulnerable.

But this is Austin Abrams’ movie, full stop, and he carries it with amazing commitment.

As Jay, Abrams is put through the wringer physically, with the camera in his face the whole hour he’s trapped inside the whale, so there’s never a moment he can't deliver an authentic reaction to what’s unfolding. He conveys so much emotion with just his eyes and some grunts (he wears a scuba mouthpiece for nearly the entire time inside the whale so he can’t speak clearly). In the scenes on land, Abrams keeps the college-aged Jay from seeming like a petulant brat, his emotional avoidance more a survival mechanism than something less mature.

items.title: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 Review
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 wastes no time hooking you into its blistering, blood-soaked world. Seriously, there are only a few minutes of speedy exposition before you're sent diving through a battered spaceship, hurling bullets and slicing rogue enemy agents to pieces – all while shouting sanctimonious battle cries as innards slosh against the tarnished metal flooring. With a breakneck pace and plenty of pixelated gore, it's clear developer Auroch Digital isn't messing with the magic in this first-person shooter sequel. Instead, the team has elevated the original's frantic run-and-gun style with boosted enemy counts and demanding level objectives that'll have you shouting 'For the Emperor.'

Boltgun 2's story kicks off with a literal bang; your ship is destroyed at the hands of the Great Daemon Vashtorr. Hungry for revenge, you respond (somewhat reasonably by Warhammer standards, might I add) by launching a brutal intergalactic campaign, fighting through bile-filled swamps to demonic dwellings, frozen facilities, and beyond. Joined by a sassy Servo-skull companion to guide you through the crimson haze, your mission is all about survival, clearing out hordes of vicious heretics while collecting enough ammunition and health kits at a cadence that's unapologetically old-school. It's repetitive by its very nature, and the story can feel a bit like Warhammer word salad at times. Still, thanks to the mesmerising enemy designs and level variety, as well as the breakneck pace, it's easy to enter a flow state of slicing and dicing through some of Games Workshop's most imposing baddies.

There are four difficulty options to work through, ranging from Low, where your health is bolstered and your damage increased, to Exterminatus, which is about as terrifying as the term would imply. For those looking for more control, you'll also have your pick of game-modifying settings like the ability to disable head bobbing and screen shake, or toggle on invulnerability, too. While I opted to play on the recommended Medium difficulty – with the campaign taking around eight or so hours per protagonist – it's nice to see Boltgun 2 accounts for all kinds of player preferences here.

While there's a lot to shout about, my favourite new feature in Boltgun 2 is the addition of a second playable character. Joining the first Boltgun's Space Marine Malum Caedo is the badass Sister of Battle, Nyra Veyrath. While both are fanatical in their devotion, as often heard in their intense, toggleable taunts, the major difference between them lies in their combat styles. Where Caedo is akin to a hulking mech kitted out with a buzzing Chainsword and frag grenades, Veyrath is much more nimble, wielding a Powersword and hefty Melta Bomb. They feel pleasantly distinct in both their personalities and weaponry. Initially, I was enamoured with Veyrath's Fervent Slide attack, which lets you blitz forward and bisect any fodder in your way, but in playing Caedo's campaign, I was equally enamored by his Chainsword Lunge, which felt more decisive and controlled, great for dealing with squishy hordes. All this to say, there really is no wrong option when choosing your warrior, and the thrill of playing as either adds to the replayability of Boltgun 2, further emphasized by the campaign's branching level options.

As you complete levels, you'll make cartographical choices throughout Boltgun 2's campaign to determine your path forward. Alongside a few optional side missions, there are specific battle locations you'll have to choose between as you advance to the big finale. On my first playthrough as Veyrath, I had to choose between dropping into a dense rainforest overrun with blight or working through a fortified beachhead with enemies hidden in sandy trenches. While I initially opted for the former, it was energizing to know that on a second playthrough, not only could I choose an alternative character with a unique loadout, but I would also have entirely new levels waiting for me.

This dynamism extends into Boltgun 2's mission objectives, too, which often have you descending into a scourge-filled hellhole to manage a few rounds of gladiatorial combat and heroically escape. It sounds familiar on paper, but each level has tricks up its sleeve. In one location, I was blowing up blood tanks to weaken a Daemonic construct, and in another, I was working my way down a vertical chamber, breaking through panes of ice to drop enemies into the blades of a whirring fan. The surprising diversity of what you're tasked with does a good job of keeping progression fresh, mitigating the dreaded shooter fatigue from setting in.

[Objectives do] a good job of keeping progression fresh, mitigating the dreaded shooter fatigue from setting in.

That's not all, though, as each map has location-specific quirks to consider. Alongside Purges, which occur periodically and lock you into areas until you've painted the floor red, certain combat conditions introduce more complexity. This time around, you aren't always alone in battle, and are occasionally joined by friendly soldiers who help keep morale high and serve as convenient meat shields when the moment arrives. Additionally, there are plenty of physical hazards, from flaming pools to thick fog that clouds your vision. These moving parts not only amp up the chaos but also create ingenious cover for Boltgun 2's well-hidden collectibles: the combat-buffing Secrets and collectible Seals.

Though for all its guts and glory, Boltgun 2 unfortunately suffers from a handful of technical issues. Enemies can occasionally forget they're in a holy war and wander around idly like NPCs. While hardly a threat to survival, it does take you out of the action to see a roughed-up creep dawdling. Elsewhere, the infamous Purges sometimes wouldn't end, and despite killing every heretic, I found myself stuck waiting for an exit to unlock… but it never did. The movement isn't completely airtight either. It's suitable for dancing around a combat arena or jumping between and scaling platforms, but it can feel slippery when tackling the more ambitious platforming challenges that arrive in the latter half of the campaign. Though it's a list of annoyances that can give cause for concern, these issues are by no means dealbreakers when set against the slick shooting and spectacle that's so distinctly Warhammer.

I have to hand it to the art team at Auroch Digital because beyond the frenetic combat, Boltgun 2's strongest asset is by far its retro aesthetic. I've spent hundreds of hours toiling over miniatures and painting intricate details to make them pop, so perhaps I have a soft spot for these characters, but Boltgun 2 captures that digitised figure look with sharp precision. The way they appear and move fits the nostalgic boomer shooter dressing perfectly. And, while it's hard to pick favourites, I can't deny that the visually assaulting Daemonettes and the towering, beast-riding Bloodcrushers were particular standouts, their violent animations and vivid palettes both delightful and terrifying. If you pay attention, there's personality embedded in almost every character model, too. As you approach them in battle, you might notice a Tormentor flicking a knife around or a tiny Nurgling mooning you mid-attack. These kinds of fine details aren't necessarily essential and could easily be overlooked, but their incorporation speaks to an attention to detail at the core of Boltgun 2 that makes it such a compelling extension of the Warhammer universe.

The atmosphere is further heightened by adrenaline-bolstering, context-specific barks that your chosen protagonist can let off at the tap of a button. Rahul Kohli delivers an impressively commanding performance in his reprisal of Caedo, and Alanah Pearce's Veyrath is fittingly vicious. Similarly, I enjoyed the writing behind the aforementioned Servo-skull, my eternally irreverent companion who would lighten tricky combat situations with lines like, "Blood Ingress detected in the ocular module." It's one thing to engage me with combat; it's another to get a genuine laugh out of me – and Boltgun 2 manages to do both.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto IV – The Legacy Review
items.author: Luke Reilly
items.content:
I’m taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t come with any new IGN score, but they will re-examine what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release. By the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly rank in my long-term love for this series.

Today it’s time to revisit Liberty City in Grand Theft Auto IV.

Grand Theft Auto IV is smaller than GTA: San Andreas. Significantly so, if you exclude water, as its land area is reportedly around only one-quarter the size of San Andreas’s physical real estate. GTA IV also has markedly reduced vehicle variety, with much fewer of them overall and zero car customisation. It has no asset management, less mission variety, no RPG-inspired skill system, a pretty paltry list of cheats, and the only thing you can alter about lead character Niko Bellic is his outfit. In fact, if you weren’t around for the arrival of GTA IV, I think it’s fair enough that you may actually find yourself a little confused about its place in the series pantheon. That is, how could this apparently smaller game with overtly fewer features than its predecessor have instantly become not only the highest-rated GTA in the history of the series, but one of the highest rated games of all time, full stop? Well, the devil is in the details. Countless, unprecedented, incredible details.

For all his faults as an Eastern European war veteran with a shady past and a short temper, who may or may not have spent 106 minutes trying to kill Owen Wilson back in 2001, Niko Bellic has actually carved out a place as one of the most likeable and accessible characters in the franchise. Lured by his cousin Roman’s lies of wealth and opportunity, it’s easy to both sympathise with Niko’s disappointment at his first encounter with the American Dream, and share in his distaste for the various bastards of Liberty City who seek to exploit him.

Released in 2008, GTA IV was the first game in the series to be set in the present day since GTA III. In 2026, it’s an interesting snapshot of the world just prior to the smartphone takeover – back when the internet was still a destination you took time out to visit on a computer, social media was still a novelty rather than the worst thing to happen to humanity since disco music, and your radio would always let you know you were about to receive a mobile phone call. However, despite the 18 year gulf between its setting and today, GTA IV doesn’t feel remotely as retro as something like GTA: Vice City did in 2002 – even though there were only 16 years between setting and the time of its release. The aesthetic distinctions between the ’80s and 2000s are, of course, profound. What are the visual differences between the 2000s and now, other than the fact The Rock used to have hair? It’s not a long list. Monoculture is dead, fashion is looping, and – as remarkably detailed as GTA IV is – I don’t think there’s anything Rockstar could have done to dodge this phenomenon, Dwayne Johnson’s shaven skull notwithstanding.

However, even though the feeling I glean from GTA IV being a depiction of a specific moment in may not be as strong as that elicited by either GTA: Vice City or GTA: San Andreas, there is no denying what a victory it is in terms of its capacity to represent a true sense of . GTA IV’s Liberty City wasn’t just one of the most convincing virtual cities of its generation; I honestly don’t think it’s an overstatement to say its commitment to tiny details still stands up to scrutiny today.

Revisiting GTA IV’s Liberty City in 2026 – a game that my Xbox 360 play data indicated to me I haven’t touched in around 14 years – I’m immediately reminded of how fastidiously crafted every corner of this world is. Yes, it’s a smaller environment than that of San Andreas, but it’s one that is so much more crowded, dense, and dripping with depth. It’s more immediate, more authentic, and more intimate than anything that came before it – and it’s still a more credible and convincing city than those in most of the open-world action games I’ve played since.

It’s still a more credible and convincing city than those in most of the open-world action games I’ve played since.

Strolling though Star Junction – Liberty City’s glitzy Times Square proxy – I find myself in tourist mode. I’m too engaged by the fact there’s something to see, read, or admire everywhere I point the camera to be distracted by the temptation of causing anti-social chaos. Hoofing it through Hove Beach – inspired by Brooklyn’s Brighton Beach – and I’m once again impressed at how much mileage Rockstar extracts from the seemingly mundane. Garbage strewn on the sidewalks. Individualised storefronts that are faithful to the demographics of the area and are never repeated elsewhere around the city. Places with stories you’ll never get to the bottom of. Like, who Mikey Pissroll, and how much better at pool he than Anal Alan?

The architecture, the lighting, the lived-in grime; Liberty City here feels more than real. It feels . Rockstar didn’t just build streets; it built them, and then assaulted that asphalt with decades of simulated wear. As a result, those streets are a patchwork of potholes, road plates, and sporadic strips of more recently re-surfaced segments. The custom signwork, the bespoke graffiti – the fact that no piece of the city looks like any other. A multitude of elements combine to create what was an unprecedented sense of immersion at the time, and absolutely still holds up today. Sure, there’s an unavoidable murkiness to playing GTA IV on original hardware like the Xbox 360, where you’re obviously beholden to the resolution limitations of its age. It results in a soft and rather muted image, and one that’s admittedly exacerbated by the overly cool and slightly washed out colour palette Rockstar opted for. However, it’s still a stunning place to simply explore, whether walking, driving, or using public transport – which is a viable and realistic way to move around this tightly-packed urban metropolis.

While Rockstar was committed to rebuilding its famous riff on New York City as realistically as possible within the fidelity it could muster at the time, it also placed an enormous emphasis on realism. The beating heart of this approach was NaturalMotion’s procedural character-animation technology, Euphoria – an animation and physics solution that completely transformed how people moved, reacted to impacts, and interacted with their surroundings. It wasn’t just a trivial technical flourish; it fundamentally altered the way the game felt to play, whether you were cutting enemies down with a barrage of bullets, or mercilessly bouncing them off the bonnet of an automobile. It reinvented GTA.

[Euphoria] wasn’t just a trivial technical flourish; it fundamentally altered the way the game felt to play.... It reinvented GTA.

Traditional animation relies heavily on pre-authored movements, with developers creating and canning specific sequences that characters will perform in particular circumstances. That is, fill them with lead and they’ll sink to the ground the same way every time. Strike them with a car and they’ll fly up and flop down identically, regardless of the forces at work. Euphoria does away with all of this and, in 2008, it felt like a stunning glimpse of the future. Ditching those pre-determined animations, characters in GTA IV react realistically – both based on the forces impacting them, and the world within arm’s reach of them. A spray of gunfire may stagger an enemy into a railing behind, which they can tumble over dramatically. A well-placed shot may cause someone to lose their balance and fall off a ledge. Clipping someone in a car will skittle them in a totally different way to clobbering them head-on. One too many drinks may make putting one foot in front of the other temporarily tricky.

The results are often wildly slapstick – like when Niko flies through the windscreen after neglecting to use a seatbelt, or when NPCs insist on clutching the door handle of your car as it begins to peel away. I still live for these moments. In fact, I’ll often hesitate before getting on the throttle to allow carjacking victims a brief window to grab on before I take them on a brief trip to destination road rash. I don’t know what that says about me. Nothing good, probably.

So much of the endless experimentation on offer in GTA IV is a direct result of Euphoria, and the fact no two encounters will ever really play out the same way twice. But it also works because it’s part of a much wider commitment to granular realism. That is, what good is a world that oozes so much character and authenticity if the people feel painted on? Like they’re skating through it rather than actually inhabiting it? Everything about GTA IV is engineered to immerse us into its world; like we’re just another living, breathing citizen of Liberty City.

Despite the incredible critical acclaim GTA IV accumulated, it remains one of the more divisive games in the series. While I am quite partial to the slower nature of its more pragmatic story and straightforward missions as a change of pace, it wasn’t to everyone’s tastes, nor was the relationship system. It was a smart way to disseminate rewards for fostering relationships with your in-game friends, but it admittedly could’ve benefited from a larger range of activities to do with them around the city – and preferably ones that were a little more fun, too. As it stands, the relationship system is too chore-like, requiring you to repeat the same cycle: pick them up, head to one of a couple of venues, and drive them home.

Similarly, GTA IV’s extremely weighty driving physics are another controversial topic. For mine, I’ve actually always been quite partial to the feel of GTA IV, particularly in certain cars where I think the exaggerated body roll and sluggish steering makes sense – like muscle cars and beefy 4x4s. I would’ve liked some more sharpness in its range of sports cars and supercars – they should have stiffer suspension as they ought to be the cars with the firmest rides – but I do much prefer GTA IV’s approach to damage modeling over GTA V.

There also doesn’t seem to be any real consensus regarding the radio stations, either, with sentiment that swings between high praise for the outright station variety to claims the song list is the most forgettable in the series. I have to concede I lean towards the latter; coming off the immense highs of Vice City and San Andreas I remember being a little underwhelmed at the time – although the soundtrack expanded and improved quite noticeably following the arrival of The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony, the two smartest pieces of DLC Rockstar ever produced.

But that’s a topic for a different day.

Sentimentally speaking, Grand Theft Auto IV isn’t my of the series – but I would say it’s the one I respect the most. It was bold to dial things back from the unhinged freedom of San Andreas in favour of a slower paced and more grounded crime saga, but it was a decision that allowed Rockstar to establish the importance of having a city so detailed it became a character itself, as well as flex a tech solution for character animation that has gone on to be a defining pillar of the series’ brand of emergent, slapstick fun. Obsessively detailed and impressively timeless, GTA IV is the prototype for modern Grand Theft Auto.

items.title: Sense and Sensibility Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Georgia Oakley’s Sense and Sensibility is one of the most eye-catching films you’re likely to see this year, but as an adaption of Jane Austen’s first novel — which she published anonymously; its authorship was originally “By A Lady” — it feels, ironically, cinematically anonymous. There’s an awkwardness to its unfolding, thanks in large part to how it engages with the novel’s tone — or rather, how it fails to — resulting in a film that barely splits the difference between social farce and genuine romance. It’s certainly watchable, but when it comes to such esteemed material, is that enough?

Sticking closely to its source, the late eighteenth century plot follows the plight of the Dashwood family — primarily sisters Elinor (Daisy Edgar-Jones) and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles) — when their patriarch dies, leaving them with little and forcing them to vacate their lush estate. Along with their mother, Mrs. Dashwood (Caitríona Balfe), and younger sister Margaret (Bodhi Rae Breathnach), the girls soon relocate to a more humble abode. Elinor and Marianne then become respectively smitten with eligible bachelors amid the complications of procedure surrounding marriage, engagement, and inheritance in Georgian England.

These societal confines determine the movie’s dramatic contours as the headstrong Elinor reminisces about her summer spent with the dashing Edward Ferrars (George Mackay), and the more sprightly Marianne becomes acquainted — by way of a classic, bumbling meet-cute — with the roguish John Willoughby (Frank Dillane) while rejecting the advances of the too-uptight Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum). As questions about the sisters’ financial compatibilities clash with the men’s white lies and half-truths, things gradually fall apart.

A key problem with the film’s unspooling emerges early on as the Dashwoods lament their lack of riches moving forward, courtesy of a selfish half-brother, the cartoonishly scheming John Dashwood (Tom Brooke), and his equally sinister wife, Fanny (Stacy Martin). For most movies, a picturesque setting backed by melodic, dreamlike strings would be an unequivocal strength, but in this version of Sense and Sensibility, the movie’s inviting aesthetics fit jaggedly alongside its borderline satirical tone, which doesn’t end up solidifying.

There are occasional jokes and exaggerations played completely straight amidst painterly visual compositions, resulting in a clumsy dissonance that leaves this iteration halfway between class satire and captivating drama. Arnaud Potier’s 35mm photography results in gorgeous natural surroundings and a sense of vivid visual contrast, but the behavior it actually captures is a tad malformed. A key element of the novel — and of previous adaptations like Ang Lee’s 1995 Oscar winner starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet — is a bubbliness underscored by a complicated sisterly dynamic. While Edgar-Jones and Creed-Miles seem to play younger, more age-appropriate versions of the Dashwoods, their personalities are reliant on exposition to explain who each of them is and why they’re apparently so different.

The filmmaking rarely emphasizes elements of their personalities; it’s a failing that becomes especially apparent during an attempt at a comedic beat when a minor supporting character, Lady Middleton (Chloe Pirrie), discusses the weather. It’s a gag meant to highlight how boring she is, but very few of the characters around her have much more life or energy to them themselves. There are certainly standouts who deliver alluring, energetic performances, from Fiona Shaw as the talkative, kindly aunt Mrs. Jennings to the Dashwoods’ larger-than-life neighbor, Sir John Middleton (Turlough Convery), but they also overshadow the leads by several degrees despite their attempts to inject the sisters’ dynamic with life and mischief.

The camera is never close enough to conjure real emotions or removed enough to highlight the era’s class absurdities. 

Oakley’s filmmaking creates a distinct sense of place and time, but the movie’s emotional moods are often at the mercy of humdrum drama lacking in judicious close-ups and other shot selections to shake things up a bit. These stilted scenes by and large play out at an unobtrusive distance of lukewarm medium shots; the camera is never close enough to conjure real emotions or removed enough to highlight the era’s class absurdities.

It’s an adaptation stuck in the middle, unable to decide between contemporary commentary on outdated social mores or full-tilt absorption into the era’s drama. Are these women justifiably aggrieved or silly for caring too much about status? You can certainly decide for yourself, but the movie’s lens doesn’t seem to gesture at one conclusion or the other despite both possibilities lingering in the ether, making it hard to be fully invested either way.

items.title: Crystal Lake Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
It’s a tricky thing, telling a prequel story. Not only do fans of the thing being prequelized know the ultimate endpoint of the tale being told, but they also already have preconceived ideas about the events happened which led to their beloved original. Essentially, the creators of a prequel already have the deck stacked against them before they ever even put pen to paper. Or, in the case of Crystal Lake – the new Friday the 13th prequel series – put knife to throat.

But then again, a prequel can work well when it understands how to color (in blood in this case) within the lines of the larger canon while also developing its own world, one filled with engaging characters, a new story worth getting invested in, and enough twists and turns to keep eyes on the screen (before a few of them are inevitably popped out or pierced). It doesn’t hurt to have a cast led by the always great (and recent Emmy winner) Linda Cardellini, either.

Cardellini stars as Pamela Voorhees, a character who your horror-fan buddy is always so proud to remind you – just in case you forgot – was actually the killer in the first , before her more famous son Jason took over in . Originally played by Betsy Palmer, Pamela was driven mad when the boy drowned at the Camp Crystal Lake summer camp due to the negligence of a pair of camp counselors, which eventually led the bereaved mother on a killing spree in that first film… before she faced her own unhappy demise.

That’s been the long and short of Pamela’s story since she debuted in the 1980 film, but now showrunner Brad Caleb Kane (who also is a writer-producer on ) and Cardellini give us a very different take on Pam. Unlike Palmer’s campy whack-job, Cardellini’s Pam is a fully fleshed-out character whom you actually root for, even as the hows and whys of her landing in Crystal Lake with her young son – yes, Jason is here – are slowly revealed over the course of these eight episodes.

It’s a bit tricky to delve into the ins and outs of this show without giving away the various fun surprises that are in store for those who stick with it, but I will say that I really had to let Episode 1 sink in before I was ready to proceed with the rest of the series. Much of this has to do with the inclusion of the 11-year-old Jason (played by Callum Vinson), who is depicted as just a regular little kid who happens to be physically, well, different from the other kids at camp. Caleb Kane and his production team manage to find a balance between the different looks of Jason that the consistently Friday the 13th movie series has given us over the decades. But it’s also a bit off-putting at first to see this little kid just being, well, a regular little kid who says stuff like “Yes, I’m reading this thing tonight!” By the time he’s raising his new machete in the air, which is part of the camping kit that Pam ordered from him, well…

But then Cardellini and Vinson get to have some really tender moments together, and you feel bad for wishing Jason was just the mute, mutated, monster from the movies. This is a prequel, after all, and you know we’ll get there eventually! And indeed, Caleb Kane reminds us of this when Jason is soon out of the picture, as cinematic fate has prescribed.

Crystal Lake does not hold out when it comes to the bloodletting, kicking off with a fairly insane fight scene in the pilot episode that goes from scary to funny and back again.

What Crystal Lake is really about, then, is how Pam goes from normal, loving mother to the not-mute, not-mutated, but definite monster that she’ll be when she one day puts an arrow through Kevin Bacon’s throat, among other dastardly acts. The character’s slow descent is methodically traced over the course of this season, as she has to deal not just with the loss of her son but also with her mysterious past which has come back to haunt her… and which she seems more than a match for, physically at least. Jason must’ve gotten his skills with a blade from somewhere!

The show populates its cast of townies and campers with various degrees of effectiveness. Cameron Scoggins as the not-too-smart Officer Dorf – a legacy character from the movies! – is a lot of fun, while Gwendolyn Sundstrom plays Jason’s young, troubled friend Grace. The latter is a character who adds a new layer to what we thought we knew about the Jason origin story; she serves as a sort of Jason stand-in for Pamela after her son is gone, for better and worse. Some of the other townsfolk are less interesting, though, and feel a bit too “supporting TV cast” for their own good.

Still, the most notable of the group beyond Cardellini is William Catlett as Sheriff Levon Brooks, who like Pam has a murky past he’d rather not dredge up, even while he can’t fully shake it. His empathy for Pam leads to a strong relationship between the two, with both actors finding different shades to play therein. How much does Pam really care about Levon, versus how much is she using him to buttress herself against any suspicion regarding the increasing number of violent incidents happening around town? Cardellini never fully lets on.

And about those incidents… Crystal Lake does not hold out when it comes to the bloodletting, kicking off with a fairly insane fight scene in the pilot episode that goes from scary to funny and back again. I didn’t keep count, but just about every episode has some kind of tour de force scene of crazy gore that will have you either gasping or chortling… or both, depending on how you feel about such things.

Caleb Kane and his writers certainly know the source material, and they cleverly write in and around events that will eventually happen in the movies (a rewatch of the original Friday the 13th in particular is worth it for fans, if not required). By the time Crystal Lake nears the end of these eight episodes, some of those same fans may be frustrated by certain developments or tweaks or additions to the overall Jason universe, while others will be gratified by how it’s all come together. But you know what they say: You can’t make a Friday the 13th prequel without killing some horny teens – or annoying a few fans.

items.title: Planet Zoo 2 Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
Running my dream menagerie in Planet Zoo is always going to feel a little different than the entertainment-focused spectacles of Planet Coaster or fantastical dino parks of Jurassic World Evolution. All of these gorgeous beasts and birds are real species we share the planet with and, in some cases, have put on the endangered list. So I was glad to see that Frontier's sequel put an even deeper emphasis on conservation as a main goal this time around, even if certain pieces of that – like wildlife reserves – feel a bit less fleshed-out than they could be.

When it comes to the daily tasks of building enclosures, hiring staff, and caring for animals, there isn't a ton that has changed since the original Planet Zoo. In that way, it feels more like a gentle evolution than a wildly ambitious one. And that's not necessarily a bad thing. If you played the first game, you should have no trouble getting your bearings in this one. There are a lot more options for adding detail, but building a functional zoo doesn't require you to learn all of them.

The species list is downright impressive, too, with over 130 creatures of all sizes to display. Some of these are exhibit-based, meaning they live in a smaller terrarium and don't have all of the same features of the bigger ones. And only around half of the list is eligible to eventually be released into the wild – more on that later. But at no point did the roster ever feel stingy. I even learned about a new species of horse!

The addition of aviaries and aquariums is the first big, shiny, new feature that isn't purely visual. And the flexibility allowed by this system is impressive. Whereas in the Jurassic World Evolution games, creating habitats for swimmers and flyers was a matter of snapping large, modular pieces together, Planet Zoo 2 gives you a lot of fine control over the shape, look, and in the case of aquariums, even depth of an exhibit.

I was really excited when I realized you can build glass tunnels through an aquarium exhibit. You can even build your entire zoo this way, as long as you stick to species that can share the same watery home without issue. Some species will fight or try to eat each other if placed together, just like in the first Planet Zoo. But there are also aquatic and semi-aquatic creatures who have different needs in terms of water temperature and salinity. If you want freshwater and saltwater exhibits in the same zoo, you even need two different filtration networks, which was an extra level of planning and realism that I enjoyed.

That brings me to the major advantage that sets Planet Zoo 2 apart from its coaster- and dino-based sister games: it's actually a challenging economic simulation. Of course, in the sandbox mode, you can turn off just about anything you don't want to deal with – from staff happiness to animal aging to the very concept of money. But as someone who very much feels that the difficulty of keeping the lights on is part of the experience, I was thrilled to find that task is not completely trivial.

If you check out my review of Planet Coaster 2, you'll recall I was deflated by the fact that I could put down one flat ride and a couple vending machines, walk away from my PC, and come back to find I had made essentially unlimited money from my sad little park. I tried a similar experiment in Planet Zoo 2, making one small exhibit with only warthogs to start and gouging my guests as much as possible to make a profit. It didn't work. And that's great!Between six different types of staff members to manage, complex guest and animal needs, and the fact that visitors can be very realistically prickly about ticket prices if they don't think they're getting their money's worth, Planet Zoo 2 has a lot to chew on even before you start moving into the rich breeding and conservation systems. There are still a couple pieces of the management screen that felt a little underbaked. Your Sustainability rating is just based on which types of power generators and wastebins you install, which is a trivial choice with no major downsides that I never really thought about again after achieving five stars before the gates even opened. But the other components of building my zoo's reputation really gave me something to strive for.

The possibilities for customization have also expanded quite a bit in that nearly all buildings now have fully-modeled interiors that guests and staff can interact with. You can design your perfect break room inside and out, and even tweak the kitchens where the animals' meals are prepared. This system goes even deeper with new, modular gift shops and restaurants in which functional seating areas and shelf displays can be placed that actually affect dining capacity and items available for purchase.I'm an absolute amateur at using these powerful tools to their greatest potential. But since the Steam Workshop once again lets me download little decorations or even whole buildings from far more talented and dedicated detailers, I can still benefit from their versatility.

There's also a campaign that serves mostly as a kind of extended tutorial. It's fine. I mainly used it as inspiration for what kinds of things I could build with the new tools. The characters still talk kind of like they're on a BBC children's program, but they're a bit less outwardly goofy this time around, which meant I had a bit more patience for them. And there is kind of a plot, even, revolving around exposing the crimes of a major corporation claiming to be environmentally friendly while actually putting fragile ecosystems at risk. It does the job well enough.

The other substantial new element of Planet Zoo 2 comes in the form of wildlife reserves, which are completely separate maps on which you paint biomes instead of enclosures, then increase their rating by introducing appropriate plants and re-wilding a variety of native species. While it can be a lot of fun to drive around in my little cart and take pictures of my zoo's former residents back in their natural habitat, the management side of these reserves feels a little shallow.

There are tons of tags for different kinds of animals that can occupy necessary biological niches on your preserves, but establishing and maintaining ecosystems wasn't always quite so satisfying. Getting rid of invasive plants, for instance, is just a matter of clicking on them with the bulldozer tool. There's no need to hire rangers or botanists to maintain the land. You're doing it all with godlike powers. I will say, I do really like the new nature brushes, which can be used to paint a variety of different canopy and understory plants with one tool. You can even make your own!

The water tools don't hold up to the same standard. There's a lot of customization in terms of surface texture, color, opacity, and so forth. But every body of water is ultimately still a fixed height, and has to be placed in a trough. It's not really possible to make something like a convincing river that flows downhill without resorting to some clever special effects that require a lot of tweaking. It made me miss the dynamic waterfalls from Jurassic World Evolution 3.

Still, it's great to have a physical place I can go visit when an animal's time at my zoo is done. I can even snap pictures of them to earn Conservation Credits, Planet Zoo 2's secondary currency that is required to adopt certain higher-tier endangered animals. I also enjoyed being able to invest my zoo's resources into new conservation projects, which offer a helpful and reliable way to turn money into Conservation Credits if you don't have any animals currently ready for release.

items.title: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
