Nearly two decades after the last mainline 2D Castlevania game,the team behind 2023’s Dead Cell’s Return to Castlevania DLC has been given the keys to Dracula’s Castle for real. Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse aims to breathe fresh life into this 40-year-old series with a creative blend of old and new ideas. With a brand new Belmont wielding the family whip, familiar foes in your way, and modern conveniences that have become expected in the genre, developer Evil Empire has largely hit their mark – but if you are a longtime fan expecting Belmont’s Curse to be a completely faithful revival of the series we played back in the early 2000s, then you will want to think again. This is a different breed of monster you're hunting, both for good and for ill.

Belmont’s Curse picks up in Paris about 23 years after the events of the NES/Famicom classic Castlevania III: Dracula’s Curse (the game Netflix’s original Castlevania series was based on). This time, the Belmont in charge of dishing out pain to the various creatures of the night – including big, bad Dracula himself – is Rose Belmont, the daughter of Trevor Belmont and Sypha Belnades. Trevor leaves Rose on her own to get to the bottom of what is going on in Paris, and the story that follows over the next 10-15 hours is one that boils down to what fans of Konami’s 40-year-old series would expect: Dracula comes back, and you need to kill him.

Belmont’s Curse does sprinkle some nifty twists into the cauldron here and there, many of which revolve around that titular “curse” and the mysterious set of Tarot cards Sypha left to her daughter before her off-screen death in childbirth. It’s a fun story overall, and I loved the nods and winks for dedicated fans like me to catch, but I’d be lying if I said plot was ever the reason I fell in love with these games.

In the line of Belmont heroes, I would rank Rose fairly high. While certainly strong-willed and focused as she sets out to prove herself worthy of her family’s legacy, you can also see she is still a bit rough around the edges. She can be impulsive at times, but learns from her mistakes – and while her tough facade occasionally cracks to reveal a more vulnerable side, Rose never comes off as a damsel in need of saving. She’d be the one busting down doors to save you. She carries the spirit of Sonia Belmont on her shoulders well.

Much like the other heroes of these games, a small cast of helpers joins her in the quest to put “Him” back in his pine box (seriously, this game really likes to lean into characters just referring to Dracula as “Him”, capital H and all). However, unlike in previous games, most of these interactions happen entirely inside of Rose’s head with the souls of bosses she has vanquished, who now find themselves sealed away in her Tarot cards. There are some fun moments of bickering between the main three – The Fallen, Joan of Arc, and Medusa – but I wish that the other bosses would more regularly chime in.

Rose carries the spirit of Sonia Belmont on her shoulders well.

I also found myself missing actual people to run into. Scenes like Alucard first encountering Maria in Symphony of the Night gave a feeling of life to the castle and its surrounding lands full of death. By comparison, the mental arguments with Medusa are amusing, but just don’t land in the same way. Considering you start out in Paris (admittedly, a violently burning one), it feels a bit odd that there isn’t a single shop open or person left to talk to. It would have been great to randomly stumble on Grant from Trevor and Sypha’s crew from Castlevania III somewhere.

The map itself is divided into large, self-contained zones, more akin to Super Metroid than Symphony of the Night, with a boss typically overseeing each area. These larger zones are then connected to one another through the odd bridge or pathway, with special ferryman doors that you will eventually uncover to allow for quick hopping between regions, including the various parts of Dracula’s castle (and other even stranger places). As someone who tends to get lost or forget things in these sorts of games, Belmont’s Curse adopts some modern conveniences that are very welcome, including percentage trackers for each area and various markers that can be placed on the map. I used these tools liberally and frequently to help keep track of blocked paths I still needed a movement upgrade to get through or collectibles I could see but not reach.

Another especially handy feature (one you are never clearly told about, for some reason) is that you are also able to fast travel between the save rooms inside a given region, done so by holding down and crouching Rose just in front of the mirror for a few seconds. This will take you to a small hub of sorts where you can choose another mirror to pop out of. For a game that has just as much backtracking and exploration as this genre is known for, it’s a great help. Too bad it takes about 15 seconds from when you first crouch until you regain control of Rose in the Hub (at least on PS5). Handy as it was, that load time got old real quick.

For the most part, each Castlevania game has some sort of unique system or mechanic that helps differentiate it. The Aria games, for instance had monster soul collection, while Circle of the Moon had its mix-and-match cards. For Belmont’s Curse, it’s largely built around a magical whip ability and a protective shield of light – and to a lesser extent, the previously mentioned Tarot cards, which grant Rose other magic spells that can be improved (she is Sypha’s daughter after all).

The whip lets Rose swing from various objects or pull herself towards them. It can also be used on enemies, allowing her to not only quickly close the distance, but, when timed with her attack, deliver stronger hits. Zipping from enemy to enemy or nimbly swinging out of the way of a charging minotaur felt (and looked) so badass, regardless of how many times I did it. There are also some pretty challenging rooms that require precision to avoid spikes and other hazards in order to reach a reward at the end, so platforming fans have something to look forward to as well.

There are some pretty challenging platforming rooms that require precision.

The light shield, on the other hand, is a far more defensive tool. When perfectly timed, it allows Rose to parry and reflect some damage back at the enemy hitting her, and also grants her the ability to pass through certain walls and floors. It’s a cool effect, but given how fast combat usually goes and how many enemies are around, Belmont’s Curse feels more tailored to keeping you on the offensive. A point further incentivized by the fact that the main way you restore your magic pool, letting you cast more spells, is by hitting enemies.

That said, Evil Empire has included several adjustable settings, such as the damage you dish out, how much experience you earn, or even the option to avoid dying altogether if you'd rather just enjoy the story.I opted to keep things mostly as they are by default with only a single exception, and it’s one I would recommend everyone make: you are able to check a box that lets you respawn just outside a boss room door if you die instead of back at a save point. To be fair, there did seem to always be a save room relatively close to the boss doors, so it doesn’t take too long to get back to the fight either way. But I much preferred being able to beat my head against a wall a lot really quickly until it breaks, as opposed to thinking of better ways to take it down between concussions. And hey, whether you love or hate boss runbacks, giving the choice to remove them or not is a great bit of flexibility to have.

Regardless of your settings, you will find many classic Castlevania enemies along the way, all sporting a rather stunning and imposing refresh in their designs. Axe Knights tower over the comparatively minute Rose while flying possessed swords spin and shoot out smaller blades to skewer you. The bosses also look great – Dracula’s right-hand man, Death, sports perhaps my favorite of his designs in the entire series and what might be the coolest scythe I’ve ever seen. But despite their sick new looks, there is a surprisingly low variety of enemies overall,with some unfortunate notable omissions. Fan favorites like Legion, the massive ball of corpses, and even iconic monsters like the wall-mounted skeleton dragon head are MIA, with Belmont’s Curse relying more on palette swaps of creatures for the stronger foes you face in later areas. There are still a solid number of different monsters, but compared to the bestiaries in other Castlevanias (even the GBA games), this one is a little disappointing.

Thankfully, what I didn’t find quite as disappointing was actually killing those monsters. Nearly all of Rose’s fighting options feel good to use, with seven unique weapon types to choose from: sword, sword and shield, spear, fists, great sword, dual swords, and, of course, the family’s signature whips. Each type comes in four tiers of strength, which are found in hidden chests or as rewards for beating the occasional boss. Up until I earned the magical Vampire Killer whip, which blew the other options I had out of the water at the time, I found myself especially drawn to the fist weapons. It was a lot of fun to pull myself to an enemy and then uppercut that foe into the air, pummeling them with fast and fierce punches that each do slightly more damage than the last.

However, while all of the combat options were cool, the more I played of Belmont’s Curse, the less it felt like what I associate with the Castlevania series specifically. The big pillars are here: you have the castle, you have Dracula and his iconic minions, you will be backtracking with new abilities to access new areas. But so much else of what usually sets this series apart within this genre has been smoothed over with Belmont’s Curse, which leaves the whole package feeling a bit like a really solid metroidvania wearing a superficial Castlevania skin. Take Rose, for example: chaining punches into air combos is a lot of fun, but it doesn’t really feel like I am playing as a Belmont. Gone entirely are subweapons like the spinning bibles, hurled bottles of holy water, or arcing axes. There isn’t even a dagger to throw, which just feels kind of wrong. She doesn’t even start the game with a whip.

The more I played, the less it felt like what I associate with Castlevania specifically.

In a similar vein, Belmont’s Curse pulls from the soulslike playbook and gives you healing vials that recharge when you visit save points (which also respawn enemies nearby), removing potions to spam. Hearts from lanterns have been replaced by sterile blue globs of mana, and now there are heart piece-like collectibles that expand your health and magic bars when you collect four. A majority of the RPG systems have been pulled out, removing most of the stats, and equipment is now relegated to just three slots for you to put relics into – those have useful but not necessarily exciting special effects, like reducing Rose’s maximum health in exchange for dealing increased damage. Heck, with all the load times I ran into, it would be nice if they at least had Rose walking through a hallway or something as a throwback to Symphony of the Night instead of a static mural. (To its credit, that mural does look awesome, but you can only stare at the same picture so many times.)

Revisiting the lands of Castlevania in Belmont’s Curse opened my eyes to how much this genre has evolved in the 18 years since Castlevania: Order of Ecclesia on the Nintendo DS – highlighted even more thanks to the wonderful collections that have been released in the past few years. We haven’t been lacking in choice when it comes to awesome action platformers like this while the series slept, either, and I would put Rose’s debut as another great option in that surprisingly long list. But while I have had a fun time with Belmont’s Curse, it also hasn’t quite scratched that Castlevania itch in the way I hoped it would.

items.title: TCL 27C2A Pro Review
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
The TCL 27C2A Pro is a Mini LED gaming monitor geared to compete with some of the hottest on the market. It offers a 4K panel with quantum dot pixels and a dual-mode that can trade off resolution for speed, much like some other high-end monitors. The TCL 27C2A Pro promises a lot, but its $999 price tag raises a lot of questions.

The TCL 27C2A Pro is a fairly tame monitor with a white-and-black color scheme that seems to chase after either Alienware’s or Samsung’s approval. Other than some RGB lighting, it’s not terribly gaudy, but it’s not incredibly pretty either.

The display squeezes in a 27-inch 4K panel that runs at 160Hz in its native mode or 320Hz when swapped down to 1080p. This kind of dual-mode technology has been popping up on more and more 4K monitors, and it’s great to see as it gives them more flexibility to serve as platforms for AAA titles with gorgeous graphical assets as well as competitive esports games where speed is almost all that matters. The panel features quantum dots and Mini LED backlighting with over 2,300 dimming zones (2,304 to be exact). That gives it a rated 98% coverage of the DCI-P3 color space and rated peak brightness of 2,000 nits — more on that later.

The TCL 27C2A Pro might have a $999 MSRP, but little about the monitor’s constructions feels like it ever should have. It builds on the earlier 27C2A non-pro model, which was cheaper and had fewer dimming zones and a lower peak brightness. But that this more expensive model was built on the bones of a cheap display makes it feel cheap as a result.

The stand and back of the monitor are covered in flimsy plastic. Though, TCL includes some colorful and modestly bright RGB lighting on the back of the monitor that at least makes it look more fun.

The monitor has an adjustable stand that gives you all the height, swivel, tilt, and rotational adjustment you’d expect from a high-end monitor, but it’s terribly jiggly. Any motion to my task transmits up through the stand. Thankfully, the monitor can be placed on a VESA mount.

Rather than having a sturdy, rigid hole through the stand for cable routing, the back of the stand has a little rubber strap that slides down to form a small loop that the cables can go through, but they don’t end up looking super tidy in practice. The monitor also uses an external power brick that you’ll need to find space for on or under your desk.

The monitor gets a couple things right in its design, at least. It includes DisplayPort and two HDMI ports. It also offers a USB-C connection that can handle video input and up to 90W of power output to a connected device. All of the ports can work with the display’s 4K/160Hz peak, though you’ll want to make sure you have cables that can do the job too.

The monitor uses a joystick for controls, which makes navigation easy. The joystick sits front and center underneath the display, so it’s easy to reach.

The TCL 27C2A Pro also includes speakers, but that should be a given in any monitor this expensive. This ensures you always have an option for audio output even when you don’t have headphones or dedicated speakers handy, so it’s a plus.

The TCL 27C2A Pro is a decent monitor for gaming, but it fails to punch up into greatness. It’s sharp and smooth, but not sharper or smoother than others on the block. Its ability to go bright can be handy, especially with its decent anti-glare qualities, but that’s about where its lead ends. Even then, sometimes the monitor just wants to go too dark.

When I tried to watch Dune, every dark scene just sank into too much darkness, leaving it hard to see anything despite the monitor’s very bright capabilities. The same happened while watching Avatar 2, with most of the movie bright and lovely but the final night of action growing incredibly dim. A few hours of Assassin’s Creed Shadows went well enough, but when I accidentally took out all the lights in a tower while fighting, suddenly I could hardly see what was on screen to make it through the combat. With local dimming, small bright elements can just about vanish on the display, too. My mouse cursor moving across a black screen dims considerably, and starfields look awful.

The TCL 27C2A Pro hits its stride when displaying bright and colorful content. Hades 2 sings, rendered in sharp fidelity and running smoothly. There’s not enough ghosting to be a bother in this game, and the color simply glows out of the monitor. There’s still some annoying artifacts from local dimming, such as certain elements (like the coin counter) appearing dim when it’s in an otherwise dark section of the screen, but these are generally subtle and hard to notice.

As things turn darker or rely more on contrast for effect, the MiniLED tech’s shortcomings next to OLED become obvious. In areas of strong contrast, such as a black and white box next to each other, exhibit a haze where the local dimming overlaps with one of the areas, dimming a portion of what should be bright white. White text on a black background can appear dim and unevenly lit. That’s rough for captions. In bright scenes, the Mini LED backlighting can definitely deliver, but black pixels close to bright elements get lifted so the actual contrast in that area will fall back to typical IPS levels. In the end, the visual quality is simply too situational.

Next to an OLED display, the differences really stand out. The whole image on the TCL 27C2A Pro is simply flattened. Little details that pop on OLED don’t have that effect on the TCL 27C2A Pro in many cases, and it’s because the contrast is neutered right where a detail should be emphasized because of the light doing the popping. This can leave things simply looking a little washed out.

Then there’s the matter of the dual-mode settings. The 4K/160Hz mode looks good, but the monitor can drop down to 1080p/320Hz for faster visuals. I saw this type of tech in action on the Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM, and it worked quite well there. Going down in resolution that much is always going to hurt a little, but the TCL 27C2A Pro looked particularly soft, with even decently sized text almost appearing blurry. It wasn’t too dramatic in the throes of battle in Hades 2, but when stopping to enjoy the scenery or read dialogue, it was more of a bother.

The TCL 27C2A Pro is capable of putting up some terribly impressive numbers when tested with a colorimeter, though. I measured its color gamut at 100% of the sRGB and 99% of the DCI-P3 color spaces. That’s just what you should expect from quantum dot color. The monitor defaults to 50% brightness, which hits a modest 167.8 nits, but if you dial it up to max brightness, it soars up to 570 nits. The wide color gamut and brightness don’t guarantee excellent visual performance in all conditions, though.

At full brightness, it achieved a 5,930:1 contrast ratio, which sounds great on paper, but the use of local dimming zones, even if there are over 2,300 of them, means the contrast depends in part on where it’s being measured. A subsequent test saw the monitor reach 8,150:1 likely due simply to a small shift in colorimeter placement. With bright squares in each corner, I even measured perfect black at the center of the display, giving it infinite contrast. But if I move the colorimeter closer to the corners, suddenly black pixels can have a few tenths of a nit bleeding through. With a 6x4 checkboard, the monitor manages a much tamer 2,038:1 contrast ratio with HDR white measuring at 693 nits and black measuring at 0.34 nits.

HDR has a lot of benefits for the monitor. It continues to cover the broad 99% coverage of the DCI-P3 colorspace alongside a comfortable 6500K whitepoint, and it can simply blast light out of a big enough area. Both a 10% window and a full white screen hit a little over 2,000 nits. That’s where its edge over OLED lies, as OLED monitors are lucky to hit half that for a 10% window and a quarter of that for a full white screen. Even a 1% window hit 975 nits. That said, smaller HDR highlights (e.g., muzzle flares or stars) will either lack brightness or lift the brightness of surrounding pixels.

The speakers on the monitor are kind of boxy and unpleasant. They put out respectable volume for casual listening, but won’t sound great for music or games, especially where spatial sound is concerned. After gaming on them for a while, they really started to grate on my ears. So, trust me, use a gaming headset.

items.title: Marvel's VisionQuest Episodes 1 & 2 Review (No Spoilers)
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
The first two episodes of Marvel’s debut on Disney+ on Wednesday, October 14.

One of the most frustrating things about the post-Endgame MCU is how long it takes Marvel to circle back around and follow up on loose ends. Heck, they waited five years between Spider-Man sequels. And that’s to say nothing of the numerous post-credits scenes that still remain unresolved. VisionQuest is yet one more example of Marvel taking its sweet time to address a character who’s been trapped in storytelling limbo. Five years after WandaVision wrapped, we finally have a series dealing with the fate of Paul Bettany’s White Vision. But it’s not necessarily Vision himself who emerges as the beating heart of the series.

WandaVision is essentially the final leg of the trilogy begun by WandaVision in 2021 and continued by Agatha All Along in 2024. When last we saw Bettany’s characters in the WandaVision finale, the regular Vision returned to blissful oblivion, while his emotionless clone fled Westview to ponder his own existence. Half a decade later, he’s still very much in the pondering phase. By day, works in a bar and struggles to master the nuances of human interaction. By night, he literally lives inside his own head in a fanciful construct populated by the various other Tony Stark-designed AI units. He’s a being who barely exists in the physical world any longer, until circumstances arise that force him back into action.

To be frank, as much as Bettany’s Vision is one of the best and most nuanced MCU characters, the series is a bit of a tough sell out of the gate. For one thing, the idyllic mansion construct feels like a rote, poor man’s recreation of what WandaVision was doing all those years ago, only without the TV sitcom conceit. It also feels like an attempted nod towards Tom King and Gabriel Hernandez Walta’s incredible 2015 Vision comic, though only in the most superficial sense. The production design in these scenes can't really be faulted, but there's nothing that WandaVision or Loki didn't do better in that regard.

On a deeper level, Vision is not at all the same character we’ve known and loved for the past 11 years. The old Vision, despite being a synthetic lifeform, was by far the most human and compassionate of the Avengers. He was responsible for some of the most poignant lines in the MCU. This new Vision utterly lacks that charm. He’s cold and distant. He doesn’t understand humans, much less feel any appreciation for their struggles and foibles. That’s the entire point of the series - the question of whether this carbon copy can gain the insight and emotional maturity that his predecessor possessed.

Now it’s Ultron who has something to teach Vision about the plight and beauty of mankind.

Regardless, this newer, less compassionate Vision is a harder character to connect with. Bettany certainly draws a firm distinction between the roles in his performance, but there’s just something a little off-putting about a Vision who shows such contempt for his fellow man and kills with abandon. By the end of Episode 2, that problem begins to recede somewhat, but there’s definitely a major adjustment period fans of the character will have to endure.

Luckily, if the series struggles to make its central protagonist fully resonate with viewers, it has a solid supporting cast to fall back upon. It’s a lot of fun seeing the various AI entities given “human” form inside Vision’s mind. That includes F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), and, best of all, the return of Agent Carter’s James D’Arcy to the J.A.R.V.I.S. role. Each character has been tasked with helping Vision understand humanity in one way or another, and all serve as entertaining foils to our dour hero.

Then there’s the real highlight of the series in Episodes 1 and 2, James Spader’s Ultron. Say what you will about 2015’s Avengers: Age of Ultron, but Spader was an inspired casting choice, and this series promises to finally realize the lingering, untapped potential of that character in the MCU. Ultron is neither entirely friend nor foe to Vision, but more a cranky, supremely bored prisoner left over from a bygone era. Spader plays the role with gusto, bringing even more gravelly, affected charm to an AI who believes himself to be the smartest guy in every room. These episodes make the most of the role reversal, as now it’s Ultron who has something to teach Vision about the plight and beauty of mankind. If it’s tough to fully connect with Vision out of the gate, Ultron alone makes the series worth watching.

That’s not to say the series is devoid of any compelling human characters. Much as Agatha All Along marked the debut of the reincarnated Billy Maximoff (Joe Locke), VisionQuest focuses a great deal of attention on his brother Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) and his own struggle to understand his existence and reconcile two very different sets of memories. Tommy makes for a compelling secondary protagonist in Episode 2, and its his presence that finally forces Vision to start coming out of his vibranium shell a bit.

On the villain front, these two episodes introduce us to Paladin (Todd Stashwick) and his handler (Diane Morgan). These two make for a fun pair, despite the fact that all of their interaction happens over the phone. In general, Stashwick brings plenty of campy energy to the screen, while at the same time molding his character into someone who feels like a legitimate threat to Vision despite the latter’s vastly superior powerset and refusal to engage in mind games.

items.title: Valor Mortis Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
I’ve gotta hand it to the people at developer One More Level: after well over a decade of countless variations on the soulslike formula, I’ll admit that going first-person with BioShock-like magical abilities shooting out of your hand in an alternate history of the Napoleonic era is… a pretty darn original idea, actually. Valor Mortis is a punishing action game that tries a whole lot of compelling stuff, from combat that mixes sword fighting, spell slinging, and firearms, to the platforming sections that have you wall-running around like you’re in Titanfall, to the bizarre 19th-century setting that kept me guessing. These experiments work out for the most part, and I have many fond memories of dying again and again as I fought my way through this bleak world full of zombified French soldiers. But there are also plenty of moments when this hodgepodge of ideas doesn’t quite come together, not to mention numerous bugs and crashes that turned an otherwise good time into my own personal Waterloo. So while the 20-hour campaign can be a bit uneven, there are still enough interesting things going on in Valor Mortis to make it well worth playing.

If you’ve ever played a BioShock game, you’ll probably feel unexpectedly at home here. Valor Mortis shamelessly cribs the channeling-magic-powers-in-your-corrupted-left-hand concept, and also has the whole alternate history thing going for it as well. But instead of blasting your way through enemies with guns, you’ll mostly be getting up close and personal with a sword, parrying, dodging, and getting killed a whole bunch in the time-honored tradition of the soulslike. It’s an odd combination of things that works out better than I expected, as using your dominant hand for swashbuckling and your off-hand for guns and magical abilities makes for exciting encounters. For example, you might use your mutated arm to light an exploding barrel on fire from afar to take out a group of baddies, block an enemy that’s aggressively rushing you, then back away to finish them off with a pistol. Having so many options for how to deal with deadly enemies helped to hold my interest longer than Valor Mortis otherwise would have, especially given its overall lack of enemy variety.

You play as William, a soldier in Napoleon’s army in an alternate reality where the legendary emperor defeated his enemies at Waterloo, which… well, caused the world to look like a disturbing piece of abstract art, I guess. As an undead warrior with supernatural powers and the ability to come back from death as many times as you need, you fight your way through a series of depressing, war-ravaged areas, meeting a few mostly forgettable characters along the way. Valor Mortis might give off BioShock vibes, but when it comes to story, it falls quite short. It delivers a fairly generic “war is hell” message that’s undermined completely by the silly stuff happening around you, like that time you’re walking in a cave and suddenly find yourself in Egypt fighting off some kind of Spinx thing? I dunno, man. In any case, I’d still say this tries much harder than the average soulslike, but ends up being mostly disappointing.

Valor Mortis’ biggest shortcoming is that, possibly because it tries so many things at once, it can be quite a rocky ride, and that includes its combat. Some of it is minor, weird stuff, like how if you’re fighting big enemies, it feels like you’re hitting them with a pool noodle from several feet away due to some really strange invisible borders. But there are also more concerning issues, like the fact that sometimes enemies will just aim their aggression in a completely different direction, attacking the air or even just standing there while you kill them. And like lots of its peers, Valor Mortis also has that issue where each of the enemies only has a few attacks, so you’ll often just be waiting for them to repeat the same series of strikes for the third time in a row before you can finish them off with an execution. While fighting these gross monsters usually feels just fine, these shortcomings crop up with regularity.

Enemies only have a few attacks, but your arsenal helps break up that monotony.

However, a decently sized arsenal of weapons and powers helps to break up that monotony. You have three different melee options, three guns for toting, and three powers to turn your poor hand into a monstrous weapon of war – each with their own upgrade tree to customize how that ability works. For example, you can upgrade your flame ability so that enemies explode if you shoot them with a gun after lighting them on fire, or you can upgrade your saber so that it restores your stamina when you attack after successfully executing a dodge.

Beyond that, you’ve also got a whole skill tree full of perks to choose from and modifiers to equip that help you customize your build a little. Perks offer ways to help William survive a bit better by upping his health or making his parries more effective, but the mods (called Ambers) are more interesting, since they can actually alter the way your character works to suit your playstyle. In my case, I equipped a bunch of mods that made it easier to top off my health, like one that healed me whenever I performed an execution on an enemy whose posture I’d broken – I then equipped another called Perfectionism, which made me do substantially more damage when I was at full health. This allowed me to be a deadly perfectionist, who was rewarded with speedier skirmishes when I successfully managed to avoid taking hits.

Most soulslikes are defined by their memorable boss fights, and this is one area where Valor Mortis feels strangely out of the loop. First off, there are shockingly few of them, to the point where you can make several hours of forward progress without running into one. Secondly, when you eventually do, they are often underwhelming, especially the ones that are just beefier versions of existing enemies or repeated foes you’ve already fought. But even when they are original encounters, they all have the same issue: you’ll mostly just stand around waiting for the boss to pepper you with a ridiculously telegraphed attack so that you can parry it and counter once you’ve broken their posture. I died way more fighting random enemies and falling off of ledges than I did against these wimpy, disappointing bosses. Frankly, it’s probably a good thing there are so few since most aren’t very memorable, and battling through each of the levels against regular minions is much more consistently enjoyable.

One of the best parts about Valor Mortis’ weird-as-heck setting is that it makes for levels that are fairly unique, like the torn-up 19th-century battlefields filled with scattered horse corpses and discarded bayonets, or a harbor of destroyed naval ships that have been raised up into the air unnaturally. You still have plenty of soulslike cliches, like one part where you navigate a flooded village overcome by toxic waters (effectively your poison swamp level if it were created by war crimes), but I was pleasantly surprised by how many areas had personality or some kind of compelling component to pique my interest. For example, one level had me creeping around a ruined town where the only survivors were children who had learned to use their small size to their advantage. Working my way through the destruction while doing my best to gain the favor of these creepy kids was a neat and memorable section that has definitely stuck with me.

Valor Mortis’ weird-as-heck setting makes for levels that are fairly unique.

Valor Mortis also tries its hand at a bit of platforming, and while I expected it to be pretty top-notch considering the studio’s track record with the Ghostrunner series, most of this sadly feels unpolished. I got caught on ledges, fell through the environment, passed through objects I shouldn’t have, and more, all of which really took the wind out of my sails. To its credit, these parts certainly try some interesting stuff, like one bit where you gain the ability to make platforms appear from afar using one of your nifty hand powers, and grappling through the air and wall running around is quite awesome when it works. But this feels like something that was a little tacked on, given how inconsistently it feels good.

I’ve mentioned a few times that Valor Mortis sometimes feels a bit janky. Some of that is due to specific game design choices and experimentation that doesn’t quite work out, but a much bigger share of that unpolished feel is due to the large amount of technical issues Valor Mortis has. I saw hard crashes, a recurring issue that straight up turned off my PC when I tried to launch from Steam, entire pieces of the environment completely missing, and tons of other wonkiness – the package just has a fairly duct-taped feel to it, which distracted from my journey through this compelling ruined world at times.

items.title: Wildwood Review
items.author: Tom Jorgensen
items.content:
There’s something wondrous about the transportive power of stop-motion animated films when they’re executed at the standard that Laika sets for themselves, and wonder is certainly the name of the game in Wildwood. Adapted from the first novel in Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis’ Wildwood Chronicles, Wildwood sees director Travis Knight and the craftspeople at Laika turning in a staggeringly beautiful and surprisingly dark fantasy adventure that boasts exciting action, enchanting and enchanted natural settings, and talking woodland creatures with jobs… and that’s all before the characters leave Portland to journey into Wildwood!

Wildwood is most impressive in its scope. As the new recordholder for the longest-ever stop-motion animated film, Knight luxuriates in building out the mythology of Meloy and Ellis’ novels onscreen. As 13-year-old Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) and her classmate Curtis (Jacob Tremblay) find themselves on a mission into the magical forest realm of Wildwood to save Prue’s kidnapped baby brother Mac, the intricate web of societies, races, and systems that prop up the setting are endlessly fascinating to keep track of thanks in large part to just how gorgeous it all looks. Laika’s films always push the boundaries of what’s possible for stop-motion animation, and the jaw-dropping artistry on display in Wildwood sees them doing it again. From the intricately authentic rendering of Portland, through each of the different domains of the massive, mystical forest, Wildwood is fathomless in its attention to fine detail.

Long stretches of the film achieve such a sense of immersion that, at its most effective, it’s easy to forget that Wildwood is a stop-motion film at all, a sensation that’s even more impressive when taking into account the wide array of fantasy trappings that Wildwood deploys.

At times, it’s surprising just how far Knight is willing to push the envelope for what could look on the surface like a kid-friendly romp.

The nature-centric magic and anthropomorphic characters Prue and Curtis come up against will no doubt feel familiar to any fans of portal fantasies like Spirited Away, Labyrinth or The Chronicles of Narnia (not to mention Laika’s own Coraline), but Knight leans into the storytelling economy afforded to him by those archetypes with confidence. The “just go with it” style of his approach to what he chooses to detail about the history of Wildwood leaves moments where the movie breezes through exposition feeling pretty inoffensive, especially in light of just how fully-realized the world feels by the end of the movie. Through it all, the stakes of the story feel very high thanks to the quickly cascading conflict Prue and Curtis’ actions set off once they cross into the wilderness. Losses feel real, setbacks have consequences and people die in this movie, and with some amount of frequency at that. At times, it’s surprising just how far Knight is willing to push the envelope for what could look on the surface like a kid-friendly romp. Sure, nothing here approaches the hellish nightmare fuel present in the R-rated, Phil Tippett-directed, but make no mistake: Wildwood more than earns its PG-13 rating.

That doesn’t stop character motivations from being occasional stumbling blocks for Wildwood, though. As fantastical and well-conceived as Wildwood’s world is, protagonist Prue does sometimes feel lost in the shuffle. Prue’s a very modern 13-year-old girl who bristles against her granola mom and dad (Maya Erskine and Jake Johnson) and takes the full brunt of responsibility for losing her brother, giving the character plenty of weight to have to shoulder as more and more bravery and pluck is required of her. Peyton Elizabeth Lee’s performance is energetic and dynamic enough to keep Prue likable, but the script doesn’t find much room for her to be more specifically defined by anything other than the wrongs she’s trying to right. That may be partially by design, maybe to let younger audience members project themselves into her adventure, but it does leave Prue feeling less memorable than the world she’s adventuring through.

The tabletop RPG-loving Curtis, still stuck on hot chocolate when his peers have moved on to coffee, plays out an expected “zero to hero” arc, with Jacob Tremblay handling the character’s comedic timing well. Wildwood’s story does take Curtis away from Prue for a lot of the movie, and the pacing tends to drag when we check back in with him and the heroic bandits he crosses paths with in enemy territory. While the record-breaking 131-minute runtime more than justifies itself from a purely visual standpoint, plot detours like this do occasionally leave Wildwood feeling a little long in the tooth.

Growing her power within Wildwood is Alexandra (Carey Mulligan), a governess of the South Wood whose grief coming out of the movie’s shockingly macabre opening scene drives her towards equally dark choices as the story goes. Alexandra’s relationship to her grief is far more interesting and believable than her machinations to quell it, but Mulligan’s quavering, edgy performance is a consistent highlight. Some late effort is made to draw parallels between Alexandra and Prue’s parents, which could’ve made Alexandra an even more compelling antagonist, but those connections don’t feel properly seeded into the early scenes to be satisfying to consider later on. From Alexandra’s grief, though, Knight does have occasion to produce some of Wildwood’s most evocative imagery, and those gothic touches are a welcome contrast to the bright, teeming life which makes up the majority of the movie’s visual identity.

What’s left to be desired by the main players is more than made up for by Wildwood’s excellently cast supporting roster of magical creatures and heroes. Mahershala Ali and Amandla Stenberg? Badass bandits! Richard E. Grant? An owl king named Owl Rex! Tom Waits? Rage-filled coyote soldier! Charlie Day? Cowardly turncoat coyote soldier! From everyone as big as Angela Bassett’s giant eagle General to as small as Awkwafina’s spunky rat Septima, the voice cast is a key aspect of Wildwood’s personality. The color each of these characters add into the mix, especially the ways the animal characters’ more base instincts peek through in their personalities, does as much to create a sense of place as any of the sun-dappled valleys or ivy-ridden ruins that Prue and Curtis traverse.

As Prue and Curtis attempt to outwit Alexandra’s forces, Wildwood’s action is breathlessly staged. The early kidnapping of the baby brother Mac by a murder of Alexandra’s crows and the chase that ensues hints at some of the gonzo camera work that’s to follow, and once the real world’s in the rear view mirror, Knight draws from every corner of his meticulously-populated frames to add a surprising twist to a fight, or to increase the danger of being caught or killed. Knight also has a pretty judicious eye for when to lock the camera into a more grounded style of coverage, and when to let it off the chain. All that excitement is very effectively supported by composer Dario Marianelli’s score, a lively orchestral bedrock which is alternatingly lead by either folk string arrangements or more modern guitar sounds depending on the environment.

items.title: Ray Gunn Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
Ray Gunn opens in select theaters on December 4 and arrives on Netflix on December 18. The film premiered on October 10 at the London Film Festival.

A 30-odd-year passion project for director Brad Bird, is a nifty sci-fi/film noir mashup that’s sumptuously designed and cleverly realized, but is slightly dinged by an overlong runtime and occasionally clunky story.

Set in the vast futuristic city of Metropia, Ray Gunn follows its titular private eye (voiced by Sam Rockwell) as he and his one-eyed alien partner, Eye-Ra (Tom Waits), investigate a case involving the world’s biggest pop star, Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson), that leads to murder, corruption and other nefarious things. If that sounds pretty gritty for an animated film from the director of The Incredibles and Ratatouille, it is.

Ray Gunn definitely leans toward a slightly older demographic than the broader audience of Bird’s past films for Pixar, which is perfectly fine since animation can obviously be more than just one kind of movie made specifically for children. While it may not be a zany animated comedy for the whole family, Ray Gunn still offers its share of cartoon hijinks for anyone who does watch it with their kids. Ray’s particle blaster pistol yields some raucous moments that would otherwise be considered body horror in a more serious film, and there’s a little alien version of essentially a French bulldog that satisfies the cute factor.

The alien designs are rather familiar but appropriate for the world these characters inhabit. The film uses some of these alien designs for humor and utility, such as Eye-Ra’s spider-like climbing skills. Other aliens are homages to film noir characters. The Jabba-like crime lord Slugsy is clearly patterned after The Maltese Falcon and Casablanca actor Sydney Greenstreet while his little henchman looks and sounds just like Peter Lorre.

The aliens who inhabit Metropia also serve as the film’s metaphor for a world where segregation and xenophobia still exist but are applied to aliens instead of humans. Aliens do all the manual labor and are banned from entering certain human facilities (for example, aliens must go to their own hospitals). There were even more avenues Ray Gunn could’ve taken to explore these serious issues a bit deeper. Unfortunately, the most noteworthy discussion about how the film explores its metaphor for racism can’t be discussed here due to major spoilers, but it was something different than an animated movie has broached before and the film handles it thoughtfully.

Ray Gunn drags a bit in the middle as the story winds its ways through the requisite beats of a detective procedural, trying to misdirect the viewer on things and characters that seemed rather obvious all along. The film, especially during its homestretch, also packs in a lot of under-explored messaging about the entertainment industry, technology and human nature without delving deeply enough to explore any of those topics beyond the cursory.

On a technical level, Ray Gunn boasts a stellar retro-futuristic aesthetic across the board, from its architecture to its costumes and gizmos and vehicles. This is a beautiful looking and sounding film (one that was especially enjoyable in a Dolby theater, so it’s a shame that most people probably won’t discover Ray Gunn until it lands on Netflix).

Composer Michael Giacchino’s moody score sounds exactly like one you’d hear in a 1940s movie, especially during more dialogue-driven or romantic scenes. All of the creative elements make Ray Gunn pulpy fun with an old-school sci-fi gloss.

The voice cast are uniformly solid across the board, with Rockwell leading the pack as the hardboiled but glib gumshoe who somehow holds on to his optimism. The cynicism that’s inherent in film noir is provided here by Eye-Ra, who Waits plays with just the right mix of world-weariness and wry wit. Matt Berry is suitably erudite but sleazy as the voice of Slugsy, while Bobby Canavale, Alan Tudyk, Michelle Rodriguez and Kether Donohue all get their respective moments to shine in supporting roles.

And it should come as no surprise that Scarlett Johansson lends a breathy sultriness to the film’s femme fatale Venus Nova, but what might surprise you is how fine of a singer she is. Composer Kimbra provides three songs for the film that Johansson performs, with “Innocent” being the biggest earworm of the group.

items.title: Soylent Green Blu-ray Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
It’s the United States of the 2020s. Climate change has created a perpetual heat wave, pollution has contaminated the air, and overpopulation combined with the consolidation of wealth and power in the hands of a select and self-interested few has resulted in major cities becoming seas of human bodies with no space and barely any resources to live. The elite can still access clean water and fresh food, but they live under guard in isolated palatial homes with women who are deprived of autonomy. The rest eat food increasingly processed and surely riddled with pathogens, and intellect and education has been eradicated for the masses, with only the elderly recalling the value of reading and academia.

So I thought: Why not watch an old favorite film instead of focusing on the real world like this? Thanks to Arrow Video, I can, through this new 4K UHD and Blu-ray release. “What is the secret of Soylent Green?” is the question asked of everyone that saw the trailer for this Charlton Heston-starring dystopian sci-fi classic way back in 1973 (concluding an apocalyptic “trilogy” for Heston that began with 1968’s and 1971’s ). But can anyone in 2026 come to this film knowing the crucial revelation upon which the entire plot relies? Maybe, since we’re now in such a fragmented era of media consumption, with people far less likely to watch the same things, not to mention that there’s even more of a tendency to ignore the old in favor of the new. If fresh eyes fall on , they may just be surprised, and I don’t want to do anything to rob them of that experience. So believe it or not, no spoilers here; it may be a futile effort, but if anyone makes any obvious jokes or references in the comments below, at least it won’t be me.

I Think It's Really Busted This Time

Charlton Heston called Soylent Green “the best B movie ever made,” but it’s so much more. At its most fundamental, the film is a noirish police procedural with a hard-bitten detective, a damsel in distress, and a global conspiracy that’s bigger than both of them. A board member of the Soylent corporation — supplier of processed food wafers like the new Soylent Green, made from plankton — named Simonson (Joseph Cotten in a very brief appearance) has been brutally murdered, and Robert Thorn (Heston) is assigned to crack the case. Police work is completely corrupt, however, so Thorn spends more time lifting luxuries from Simonson’s opulent pad and availing himself of the “furniture,” otherwise known as Shirl (Leigh Taylor-Young) — one of the many women in this world whose life has been reduced to domestic imprisonment and sexual servitude in apartments occupied by their elite masters. With Simonson dead, Shirl will soon meet the new tenant that she’ll be required to serve; for now, at least, she has Thorn.

This is a relentlessly moist movie; to convey the oppressive levels of heat, the entire cast is drenched in stage sweat except when in the domains of the wealthy (and a certain elderly-centered facility late in the film). The movie is also largely drab and awash in beiges and grays, but the color palette pops when necessary with bright saturated colors that really shine on this new release, whether it’s a rare strawberry or a blue dress. It looks beautiful and rich, but with a grain that feels right for the period; I’m not sure if it was always there, but there’s an additional haze that looks particularly appropriate and oppressive whenever we’re outside in the heat, with a greenish tint that reminds us Soylent Green is omnipresent.

The movie is also a masterclass in world-building, beginning with a montage created by Charles Braverman (based on his 1968 short film, “American Time Capsule”). With bombastic music by Fred Myrow (whose scoring is kept minimal in the rest of the film), the rapid-fire depiction of the country’s industrial development and degradation sets the Soylent-laden stage. Opening scenes set in Thorn’s apartment juxtaposed with the home of the wealthy Simonson perfectly delineate the ways in which the two main tiers of society operate in this far-flung future of 2022, as well as the kinds of relationships that define their lives.

(And yes, Star Trek: Deep Space Nine drew on this concept for their two-part episode, “Past Tense,” and even referenced soylent in prop posters. And yes, the film’s co-star Brock Peters is Sisko’s dad on DS9. Moving on…)

We've Gotta Stop Them… Somehow

Despite being part of a deeply damaged system, there’s a nobility to Heston’s Thorn and a dedication to the truth that drives him to actually do his job. Much of that comes from his long-term father-son relationship with his “book,” Solomon Roth (Edward G. Robinson), an elderly former college professor and live-in research assistant who provides Thorn with crucial investigative support. Their bond provides the emotional core of the movie, no doubt at least partially informed by their previous work together in The Ten Commandments (1956) and the original makeup tests for Planet of the Apes, where Robinson played Zaius (he dropped out of the actual film for health reasons). Thorn’s relationship with Chief Hatcher (Brock Peters) is another great touch. Hatcher relies on his colleague and friend to regularly fix his watch, and Thorn tinkers away, thus letting us know he’s rather smart for this world too… but only to a point. When he finally admits he can no longer repair the watch, it’s symbolic of something much larger; there are some things that will be beyond his ability to fix.

The moment when Thorn hears the secret of Soylent Green (but the audience doesn’t yet) from Sol himself and is moved to tears will haunt you for days afterward.

The film features a solid supporting cast that all add so much to even the smallest roles, including former Rifleman Chuck Connors as bodyguard Tab, the mesmerizing Paula Kelly as Tab’s girlfriend (roommate?) Martha, and the unctuous Leonard Stone as the apartment manager/pimp, Charles. In particular, fellow Omega Man alum Lincoln Kilpatrick turns up as Paul, a priest with knowledge that’s eating him away from within, and he even gets to reference the title of the 1966 Harry Harrison novel that serves as this film’s inspiration, Make Room! Make Room! Celia Lovsky (Vulcan matriarch T’Pau from the Star Trek original series episode “Amok Time”) also appears as the leader of the Exchange, where Sol and other “books” meet to share sources and information. She gets to tee up the obligatory “is Chuck actually God” joke, and when Sol brings her a rare volume never seen by the Exchange before, her trembling hands reaching reverently for the cover of the book is so evocative of everything that’s been lost.

But in many ways, this is Robinson’s film. A scene in which he eats real food with such relish and then realizes how profoundly sad it is that they’ve come to this state is a study in expertly modulated acting. The veteran actor knew he was dying even as he completed his last role — he passed away two months after finishing filming — and he brings every bit of experience and pain to a beautiful performance that also seems to push Heston to up his game. As a bookend to the film’s expertly-crafted opening, the film’s finale is a harrowing journey to the truth that begins when Sol makes a fateful decision that leads him and Thorn to the conclusion of the investigation and the movie’s big reveal. There’s a moment during that final sequence, when Thorn hears the secret of Soylent Green (but the audience doesn’t ) from Sol himself and is moved to tears; it will haunt you for days afterward.

While there is a new 2025 commentary track recorded for Arrow with film historian Michael Brooke and author Johnny Mains, there aren’t many other extras here you wouldn’t have encountered in previous releases of the film, including image galleries, the trailer, vintage featurettes about the making of the movie and its landmark position as Robinson’s 101st film, and an archival 2003 commentary track with director Richard Fleischer and actress Leigh Taylor-Young. Fleischer covers the thematic and production elements, while Taylor-Young chimes in to discuss her environmental work at the UN, her view of the film as a “harbinger,” and her attempt at a Ten Commandments joke during her shower scene with Heston. You can hear Heston briefly discuss the film during an audio-only 1985 BFI appearance, while Fleischer touches on it in a 1994 BFI interview captured on video that also covers his memories of the blacklisting era.

Perhaps most significant, however, in terms of additions for this new release is a booklet presenting material written by Dr. Alexandra Heller-Nicholas (who I recently encountered via her superb contributions to Severin Films’ Sangster Directs Hammer box set). I’d to tell you more about it, but I , because Arrow didn’t provide an actual release copy for review. It was very nice to at least receive the screener disc, but as these reviews are about celebrating and supporting physical releases, that includes all aspects of the presentation. I have to assume Dr. Nichols’ work is exemplary as always; her attention to detail and respect for history is surely better than Arrow’s, which sent an accompanying press release listing other classic ’70s sci-fi films “Wetworld” and “The Andromeda Syndrome.” JFC, Arrow.

items.title: Avatar: Seven Havens Episodes 1-3 Recap and Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
This review contains full spoilers for Season 1, Episodes 1-3, which debut October 9 on Paramount+.

The experience of watching the first new Avatar series in 12 years — Avatar Aang movie and Netflix’s live-action adaptation aside — is an overwhelming one. While there have been numerous (pretty excellent) comic book tie-ins and extensions released in the intervening decade plus, insuring that the world created by Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko has never fully gone away, they’ve all felt like mere footsteps from the stellar runs of Avatar: The Last Airbender and The Legend of Korra — reinterpretations of information we already had on hand instead of something really new.

Avatar: Seven Havens, on the other hand, really truly new. Set 225 years after the events of Legend of Korra in a post-apocalyptic landscape where all that remains of humanity is based in the Seven Havens of the title, the show evolves the animation style and setting in a way that’s closer to Miyazaki or recent surreal hits like Scavengers Reign or Common Side Effects rather than what we might expect from an Avatar series.

But even with the different animation, there’s something both alien and familiar about watching Seven Havens. On one hand, you’ve got a kid Avatar in Pavi (Saheli Khan) — more on that in a second — just like Aang in the original series. But unlike Aang, who had a very clear path forward (stop the Fire Lord, save the world), Pavi has been living on the outskirts with only bugs, rocks, and her cat-monkey (voiced by Dee Bradley Baker, the voice of Appa and Momo in the original series) as friends, with no clear path to saving a world that maybe doesn’t to be saved.

The sly humor that DiMartino and Konietzko have woven into previous series is back, and an early sequence in the premiere, “On The Horizon,” with Jae (Major Curda) surfing his way through the Haven of Ellora is an utter delight. But if Korra took the franchise in darker, more adult directions, Seven Havens is both a reflection of the world we live in today and of the anger some fans felt toward the character of Korra. The plot involves something Korra did two centuries earlier that broke the world, leading to the survivors hating and fearing the Avatar; it’s also clear in the first three episodes that this story isn’t done, and it also isn’t what the world thinks. It’s just speculation, but it very much feels like DiMartino and Konietzko are saying, “Oh, you hate Korra so much? Well, here’s why you’re , and we’ll lay it out for you over the course of 26 episodes.”

That aspect could be a little (well, a ) navel-gazing, but there’s the outward focus the creators are bringing to the story as well, diving harshly into both the divided nature of our own real world and the coming climate apocalypse. Animation is never going to have the pace necessary to really reflect the world outside our window — it usually takes at least two years for an animated season to make it from script to screen, unless you’re South Park — but thanks to an Avatar classic (a play at a festival performed by children), we discover why the world hates the monster Korra and how the Seven Havens were formed together but now stand far apart. In the third episode, “The Order,” the airbender Karthik (Akshay Khanna) — now promoted to Commander of the Bending Brigade in Ellora — suggests they reach out to the other Havens as fewer and fewer benders are being born every year. He’s flatly turned down: Ellora can stand for itself.

This isolationist stance has been bubbling over in our real world for a long time now, and it’s hard not to watch scenes like that without thinking about Brexit or America’s increasing push to close its borders. Similarly, the threats in the first few episodes — other than a menacing red diamond; more on that in a second — are all climate based. A tornado is the “villain” of the premiere, and a massive green storm nearly destroys Ellora in Episode 2, “Into The Storm.” Again, it’s not one to one, but with our own climate disasters increasing year by year, it’s clear that DiMartino and Konietzko are setting up Seven Havens as both a commentary and a warning, while also delivering a fun mythology-building Avatar series.

Seven Havens is set up as both a commentary and a warning, while also delivering a fun mythology-building Avatar series.

Speaking of mythology-building, the first two episodes essentially function like one pilot, and are surprisingly sparse on action and plot… laudably so, as the series in those initial 40ish minutes sits in the silences and lets us feel what the characters are feeling instead of thrill at Cool Bending Fights, though there are plenty of those too. The two plot tracks follow Pavi as she rides her cat-monkey, trying to hide while a festival celebrating the rise of the Seven Havens takes over Ellora; and Jae as he works with his bending team from the town’s Bending Brigade to help fix a crumbling bridge.

Pavi is, per the title of “Book 1,” all about survival and that’s it. Jae also ties into that theme; he’s focused on protecting Ellora to a fault, though having been raised in a post-Avatar society, he doesn’t seem to understand what he’s protecting or why. When Pavi ends up accidentally causing havoc at the festival by freeing some bugs, she uses her earthbending and alerts Jae to a rogue bender. Traveling out into a storm, Jae appeals to Pavi with kindness, but they get interrupted by a tornado, which Pavi helps shut down by revealing she can also airbend. This reshapes Jae’s whole thinking: What if the Avatar a monster, but in this case a nine-year-old girl with one leg who’s just trying to live?

Jae brings her back to headquarters to try and figure out what to do, trusting his superior Karthik with the info, while Pavi sneaks off only to discover Avatar — specifically, her twin sister Nisha (Aishu Devan). Shouts to Paramount for doing a good job hiding this secret despite it being pretty obvious that front-loading twins as the main characters of the series would imply they’re the Avatar. Given what we find out shortly — that Nisha has a lot of Korra’s impulsiveness and anger in her, while Pavi has Aang’s wackiness while being all refusal no call — it’s a neat way of splitting and analyzing what made previous Avatars work (or not) thanks to the twins.

It also kicks us into our central mystery in Episode 2: Who Pavi and Nisha, why don’t they remember each other, and how are they the Avatar — the first time in the Avatar cycle that two people have held the title at the same time? Shades of Buffy and Faith on Buffy the Vampire Slayer, perhaps? Rewinding time, we get to see a little bit about how Nisha has been training in secret under the guidance of Karthik and desperately wants to go out and help. She gets her chance thanks to the aforementioned giant green storm.

While we get to see Ellora activate the Bending Brigade to mitigate the damage of the storm, which is pretty neat, the focus is on Pavi and Nisha, who eventually join together to help, only to be confronted by a strange red, pulsating diamond crackling with evil-looking energy. After it does to Karthik’s commander, who fled at the sight of it, Pavi and Nisha manage to trap it, only for the diamond to envelop them, send them to another dimension, and then hit them with what are likely missing memories. The diamond then disappears, leaving behind red crystalline structures throughout the wrecked Ellora, and again it seems pretty clear that this may not be evil so much as something reaching out — likely from the Spirit World, and potentially even an aspect of Korra; TBD on that.

This brings us to Episode 3, which thanks to an opening title sequence laying out the plot in classic Avatar style — thank goodness; it was missed in the first two half-hours — feels like the first real episode of the show. The main thrust here is that Jae is completely melting down at keeping the secret of the re-emergence of the Avatar(s), while Pavi and Nisha are at odds over doing Avatar training with the surprise return of the Order of the White Lotus, a group of wise men and women who often will help guide the Avatar. This comes together when the three characters all calm what looks like an armadillo-camel that’s been corrupted by the red energy; it acts like a pill bug rolling around Ellora, and we’ve had armadillo-bears and armadillo-tigers before.

Here we get key component of the series — the . Jeremy Zuckerman returns after working on The Last Airbender and Legend of Korra, and he’s created a heart-aching, gorgeously poignant score for the series, particularly the theme that haunts Pavi and Nisha in the first two episodes. But it isn’t until Episode 3 when Pavi plays the theme on the kalimba that it becomes clear what the real purpose of the score is. Memory is spurred on by music, and the song we’ve been hearing for two episodes so far is actually a song that Pavi and Nisha’s mother used to sing to them, complete with lyrics. It’s a goose bump-inducing moment when this is revealed, as the duo sing together on instinct, calming the animal and sparking various memories.

If there’s a criticism to be made here, it’s that it’s hard to tell exactly where this is all headed. We do get an indication when Pavi and Nisha discuss needing to go find their parents, and if this is a more emotionally driven story than the world-ending stakes facing Aang, or the threats to Republic City — and sometimes the world — that plagued Korra, it should be an interesting swerve. The show already tugs at your heartstrings from the opening moments, so this viewer at least is invested in seeing Pavi and Nisha find happiness.

Maybe as our own world has gotten murkier and more confusing, the world of Avatar has as well.

But we’re also three episodes in and have thus far encountered one (1) Haven, and even with the show just starting, you can feel time ticking away. It’s also laudable to deal with a climate apocalypse, but a green storm, a tornado, and a red diamond are not exactly the terrifying and complex villains this franchise is known for. Perhaps that’s coming: Demon-masked antagonists show up right at the end of the third episode, and likely will spur our three main characters to flee and explore more of the world, thus setting up our stakes. Maybe as our own world has gotten murkier and more confusing, the world of Avatar has as well. There’s no one evil bad guy you can defeat to save the world; it’s up to the next generation to fix things as best as they can.

These are minor quibbles when it feels so good to get back to this universe with new characters, new settings, dazzling animation, and soaring music. Welcome back, Avatar; yip yip.

Avatar Easter Eggs, References, and Connections

While most of the easter eggs and references in these episodes are pretty blatant, it might be helpful to lay some of them out for more casual viewers (or since it’s been, you know, well over a decade). Let’s start with the play about Korra performed by a bunch of kids in the town square of Ellora. Plays have been built in since “The Ember Island Players” debuted in The Last Airbender Season 3, showing off the adventures of the characters in the series via a ridiculous play titled “The Boy In The Iceberg.”

In Episode 2, Karthik reveals the lost history of the Avatars — everyone only knows Korra — and shows off a scroll depicting the older Aang with the dumb chin beard as seen in Legend of Korra, Avatar Kyoshi, and Avatar Roku. There are, FYI, a more Avatars than that, including some secret ones that were revealed in the Avatar Aang movie.

In Episode 3, we also get to see some pictures of previous members of the Order of the White Lotus. The beloved Iroh is right in the middle, with Jeong Jeong to his right and Pakku to his left — all three members of the Order during the time of The Last Airbender. Curiously, it’s harder to identify the waterbenders on the left and right side of the display; the woman all the way on the left could be Katara, but she doesn’t have the icon’s little hair loops. Other waterbenders known to be part of the Order include: Ayunerak, aka Mama, who appeared in The Dawn of Yangchen novel and has never been seen visually; Kavik, also from The Dawn of Yangchen, who has a very handsome picture but doesn’t look like the guy on the right otherwise; Ivalu, from — you won’t believe this — The Dawn Of Yangchen; and Aupilaarjuk, who was from Kyoshi’s era and only appeared in the Avatar Legends role-playing game. Sadly pictured on the wall of fame is crazy old Bumi, the earthbending King of Omashu.

Also of note? The entire Haven of Ellora seems to be laid out like the symbol for the Order, which certainly implies a lack of coincidence in the Avatars ending up there. That said, we have yet to see the other six Havens, so maybe they’re all laid out the same with their own divisions of the Order.

Less an easter egg than a nice, progressive note: Jae has a boyfriend named Datu (Topher Ngo). While things don’t go further than some embraces and a kiss on the cheek, this is a far cry from the surprising swerve of Korra and Asami getting together in the final seconds of Legend of Korra, a move that was lauded (yay representation!) and lambasted for its execution (the quickness and generally unclear way they “got together”). Baking in Jae and his boyfriend right in the third episode seems like a clear way to be more explicit about the inclusive world of Avatar. Similar to DiMartino and Konietzko stepping back and letting more racially appropriate voices write, direct, and act, this shows a welcome growth from where they were a decade ago; they’ve clearly been listening and learning.

Finally, let’s talk about that odd red diamond. The dark energy does seem to be some sort of conduit to, or from, the spirit world, and given that we don’t know what Korra did or how Pavi and Nisha connect to this — or why there hasn’t been an Avatar in centuries — it raises a lot of questions we’ll surely explore as the show continues. Let’s throw out a crazy idea here: What if this Korra’s fault; what if was ? This is something that was dealt with before in Legend of Korra, but there’s something about this energy that’s reminiscent of energybending, the forbidden practice that Aang used to take away Fire Lord Ozai’s bending at the conclusion of The Last Airbender. Is it possible Aang broke something there that Korra was trying to fix, rather than the other way around? This is pure speculation, but why not? We’ve got plenty of episodes to be way off about these theories.

items.title: Cupertino Season 1 Premiere Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Full spoilers follow for the season premiere of CBS'

The world is a little bit easier to take when there’s a topical drama by Robert and Michelle King on our televisions. From thorny legal battles (The Good Wife, The Good Fight) to religious conundrums (Evil), the Kings have tackled some of the more complex issues in modern life with humor, pathos, and realism. Gratefully, they’re back to help us parse the current tsunami of tech threats from pervasive AI to infringed privacy with Cupertino.

"Michael & Olivia" opens with Silicon Valley lawyers Michael Price (Mike Colter) and Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller) separately getting unceremoniously canned by their tech start-up employer, S-Talk. Michael is an equity co-founder, while Olivia is a junior lawyer one year out of law school, but getting career-dumped is today’s great equalizer. As they awkwardly commiserate on the curb and share some genuine admiration for one another’s work, Olivia throws him an information bone because he’s always been nice to her. While working with owner Richard Everett (Will Brill), she heard him asking someone how to fire an equity partner for cause while keeping their money… meaning Michael was unlawfully pushed out.

From that little moment of allegiance blooms the duo who are the beating heart of Cupertino. Colter’s been a ride-or-die actor for the Kings going back to The Good Wife, and here he brings smarts, charisma, and simmering sex appeal to Michael Price. Though this character wears tailored suits and comes from a prestigious family of lawyers, Michael is a believer in the Davids battling these tech Goliaths, which keeps him grounded and empathetic. The yin to his yang is Rachel Keller’s Olivia, who is shrewd yet green. Post law school, she migrated straight to Silicon Valley from the sheltered arms of her rural Christian family, so there’s plenty for her to navigate as she starts swimming with the sharks. Fresh from the series , Keller was also stellar in FX’s so it's exciting to see her go toe-to-toe with not only Colter but Cupertino’s ever-expanding ensemble of top-notch recurring actors to come, including Girls5eva alums Busy Philipps and Renée Elise Goldsberry, Joe Morton, and Jackie Earle Haley.

If you’re an existing fan of the Kings’ work, Cupertino feels a little like comfort television because it utilizes many of their signature storytelling elements: ripped-from-the-headline cases; the casting of theater-great character actors; storylines that breathlessly twist on a dime; and their ability to make serious subjects comprehensible, weird, and entertaining. They’ve even 2.0’d their The Good Fight lady fixer character Marissa Gold, updating her as Michael and Olivia’s Gen Z street-smart office manager, Christy Palladino (Ella Stiller).

Cupertino reminds us that there’s no shame in being a broadcast procedural when you’re working at the level of the Kings and their collaborators. 

Yet familiar doesn’t mean this is a dumbed-down procedural by any means. The Cupertino pilot alone tackles tech industry sexual harassment and equity disparity, stealing personhood for LLMs, and the fragility of tech bros with their shell games and unethical smoke screens. It’s all presented with wit and intelligence, and through characters who bring us into this alien world of stealth technology and can decipher this industry that's moving too fast and breaking things with seeming impunity. Cupertino reminds us that there’s no shame in being a broadcast procedural when you’re working at the level of the Kings and their collaborators.

If The Good Wife and The Good Fight could give me an understanding of Constitutional law and systemic governmental flaws, I can’t wait to see what the Kings school me on with Cupertino.

items.title: HBO's War: Season 1, Episode 2 Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
After a heavy dose of frenetic table-setting in , War’s second episode — sharply written by George Kay and deftly directed by Ben Taylor — slows its pacing down a bit as Morgan (Dominic West) and Carla (Sienna Miller) and their respective legal teams enter the pivotal three-day mediation period of their divorce.

Morgan and Carla are each instructed by their teams to put on amicable fronts as both sides strategize how to strike the best deal. That means a lot of strained smiles and literal hand-holding between the divorcing spouses to mask any anger and bitterness. Their facades just barely hold. Behind the scenes, their teams are reckoning how to protect their clients and gain the upper hand.

After Carla was surprised on the red carpet with divorce papers, her lawyers at Taylor & Byrne want to control the developing narrative, namely the matter of Flora Monroe (Rose Williams), the young actress Carla enlisted to honey-trap Morgan in a one night stand.

Taylor & Byrne partner Serena (Phoebe Fox) tries to convince Flora to sign an NDA as a means to protect herself and Carla, but Flora is unnerved by the request. She’s not fond of being paid off as if she were a prostitute. Flora insists she chose to sleep with Morgan because she found him attractive.

Serena’s plan ends up backfiring spectacularly because her new hire, Johnny (Archie Renaux), is secretly on his first assignment as the mole for Morgan’s lawyers at Cathcarts. Johnny is funneling information to both firms about Serena’s offer to compensate Flora and detailing the shakedown engineered by Flora’s greedy mother Mumsy (a scene-stealing Camille Coduri). Needless to say, things are getting messy and murky for everyone as both legal teams play dirty.

Then there’s the curious implication that Johnny is growing romantically (or just sexually) interested in Carla and/or Flora. He hasn’t outright said anything but his search history and longing looks don’t lie. Johnny seems poised to not only screw up his relationship with his girlfriend Bella (Honor Swinton Byrne) but the entire divorce case for both firms.

Flora also seems ready to make things even worse for herself by texting Morgan in the episode’s closing moments. Is she playing her own separate angle or does she legitimately want to be with Morgan romantically again? We shall see.

West and Miller excel in this episode at smiling through their teeth at each other, while Renaux continues to find the humanizing nuances in the double-dealing Johnny. Fox’s Serena seems like the closest thing to a good guy in this story, but there’s enough iffy moral resolve in her that maybe she will end up surprising viewers with an eventual turn to the dark side.

As Serena’s adversaries Beatrice “Queen Bea” Ubosi and St John Smallwood, respectively, Nina Sosanya and Pip Torrens continue to be a great one-two punch duo who find enough wit and aplomb in their predatory characters to put the guilty in guilty pleasure.

items.title: Other Mommy Review
items.author: CarlosAMorales
items.content:
Other Mommy is in theaters now.

Although she’s made her reputation (and her Academy Award) on prestige dramas, Jessica Chastain is no stranger to horror. The Sacramento-born thespian has starred in the likes of Mama, It: Chapter Two, and the underrated Guillermo del Toro joint Crimson Peak, and once more returns to the genre with , a new film from director Rob Savage where Chastain plays the dual role of a mother and her demonic doppelganger. Sadly, the film wastes what should be a slam dunk premise (and a trailer that based on a well-timed jump scare) on a generic script and not enough ideas to fill out even its brisk 90-minute runtime.

Arabella Olivia Clark stars as Bela, a seven-year-old girl living a not-quite idyllic suburban family life with distant mother Ursula (Chastain) and doting father Russell (Jay Duplass). There’s some tension in the home stemming from Ursula’s seeming workaholic lifestyle that Bela is already aware is actually a cover for her mother having an affair, but not enough that her parents haven’t been blissfully unaware that Bela has been hanging out with a not-imaginary friend named Other Mommy (also Chastain). Other Mommy loves spending time with Bela when Ursula can’t be bothered but also won’t stop insisting that Bela agree to let Other Mommy “into her heart,” the outcome of which is assuredly some form of demonic possession but also isn’t explained enough for the audience to dread it.

What follows is a surprisingly quick acknowledgment from Ursula and Russell that something supernatural is going on, and the family fleeing their home to locale after locale where Other Mommy inevitably arrives to cause more mystic mayhem.
